manopt `symmetricfactory`. Packed row-major `n^2`. Projection is
symmetrization, retraction is `X + U`, transport is the identity.
A 3N cluster is rejected. Stamp layout 4.

`xts.h` declares the exported `rgmin_minimize` / `rgmin_solver_*`
symbols; `xts_minimize` and `xts_solver_*` are macro aliases.

L-BFGS session `Accept::None` takes the clipped two-loop
direction. Wolfe line search stays on Energy / Nonmonotone.

SCG C waist: closed `xts_conjugacy_t` on `xts_scg_params_t`
(FR`0 .. FrPr`7, dest leaf order). `params==NULL` is Netlab
Polak-Ribiere. Unknown codes are `RGMIN_INVALID_PARAMETER`.
Stamp 1.13.3. Hybrid and Restart stay Rust-only.

Typed lowest-mode waist: closed `EigensolverKind` (Lanczos=0
through EigenExa=13, `schema/eigen.capnp`) and `EigenParams`
(`nev`, `krylov`, `max_iter`, `tol`). No Text. C
`rgmin_lowest_eigenpair` plus `rgmin_eigen_params_t`. Unlinked
backends return `RGMIN_UNAVAILABLE`.

Molecular manifolds: `rigid_quotient` is Sella Cartesian
`R^{3N}/SE(3)` (`fix_translation` + `fix_rotation`);
`mw_rigid` is the Page–McIver / Sella IRC Eckart metric on the
same quotient (`rgmin_solver_set_masses`). SO(3) is length 9 and
SE(3) is length 12; a 3N cluster is rejected rather than packed
or prefix-interpreted. Periodic bulk sets
`rgmin_solver_set_periodic`: Sella `proj_rot = false`, quotient
`R^{3N}/T(3)`. Isolated stays `R^{3N}/SE(3)`. `abi_minor` 10.

Opt-in `Lbfgs::minimize_box` and `Lbfgs::minimize_box_watched` relax inside a box `lower <= x <= upper` with the generalized Cauchy point and the subspace minimization of L-BFGS-B (Byrd, Lu, Nocedal and Zhu 1995).
Each direction ends at the subspace minimizer from the Cauchy point, and the strong Wolfe search stops at the box.
`Lbfgs::minimize` keeps the eOn cap. `LbfgsStep::Wolfe` remains opt-in.

An interior point skips the bounds clip, and a Euclidean session keeps the gradient it already owns.
Polak-Ribiere forms `g · (g - g_old)` in the dot product.
A backtracking line search keeps its lowest trial without copying that vector.
FIRE 2.0 does not build the post-step force, which only FIRE 1.0 mixes.
L-BFGS reuses the curvature dots stored with each pair.
The Morse-chain iterates are unchanged.

The default L-BFGS step follows the eOn client, including the finite-difference curvature probe and `distance_reset`.
A proposal at least as long as the cap clears the memory and steps along `H0` times the force.
`LbfgsStep::Scaled` and `rgmin_solver_set_lbfgs_scaled` keep the previous shorten-and-retain rule.
`Conjugacy::PolakRibierePlus` is SciPy's `max(0, β_PR)`.
`Restart::powell` is the eOn conjugate-gradient restart at 0.5, and the method token is `eon-cg`.
Hager-Zhang applies the CG_DESCENT floor.
FIRE 1.0 treats a zero power as downhill.
The comparison is `bench/results.md`, with the raw rows in `bench/raw/`.
`abi_minor` 35.

L-BFGS does not line-search by default.
The default step is the eOn cap: the longest atom moves at most `EON_MAX_MOVE` (0.2), `H0` is the Nocedal-Wright scale `(s · y) / (y · y)`, shortened steps keep their pairs, and a direction that is not descent clears the memory.
`LbfgsStep::Wolfe` and `rgmin_solver_set_lbfgs_wolfe` opt into the strong Wolfe search.
`abi_minor` 34.

`benches/ase_h2h.py` compares ASE 3.29 LBFGS, FIRE and BFGSLineSearch with rgmin capped L-BFGS, Wolfe L-BFGS, the geometry step and FIRE 2.0.
The starts are LJ7, LJ13, LJ38 and the periodic Morse cluster of 256 platinum atoms.
Every arm uses fmax 0.01 and maxstep 0.2.
The table is `benches/ase_h2h/results.md`.

`LbfgsStep::Capped` is the atomistic L-BFGS step, and it is the default.
It drops the line search.
The two-loop step is shortened so the longest per-atom displacement is at most the caller's cap, and the initial inverse Hessian stays the Nocedal-Wright scale `(s · y) / (y · y)`.
An empty memory steps along the force at that length.
Pairs are kept when the step is shortened.
`set_atom_maxmove` selects the geometry step only after `LbfgsStep::Wolfe`.
`Solver::set_lbfgs_step` installs the rule on a Euclidean L-BFGS session.
The C header declares `rgmin_solver_set_lbfgs_capped`, the C++ wrapper has `set_lbfgs_capped`, and `xts.h` aliases it.
`abi_minor` 33.
`cargo run --release --example lbfgs_capped` prints the force calls and the median wall time.
@@rst::doc:`reference/sota`@@ records that run.
On LJ7 and LJ13 at atomic force 0.01 the geometry step uses fewer evaluations at the same energy, and on the extended Rosenbrock function with four or more coordinates the value near 3.98 is a local minimum in the basin of `(-1, 1, ..., 1)`.

`Lbfgs::ftol` is the opt-in relative-decrease stop of L-BFGS-B, and its default of zero turns it off.
A line-search step from `f_k` to `f_{k+1}` ends `minimize`, `minimize_watched` and `minimize_recognized` when `f_k - f_{k+1} <= ftol * max(|f_k|, |f_{k+1}|, 1)`.
`LBFGSB_FTOL` is the SciPy default, and @@rst::doc:`reference/sota`@@ measures what it saves.

`Solver::set_distance_constraints` keeps atom pairs at fixed distances on every session method except particle swarm, under every `Accept` rule.
`DistanceConstraints::at` takes the lengths from a geometry, and `DistanceConstraints::new` takes them as given.
Each trial returns to the set through the Gauss-Seidel bond solver (SHAKE) or the linear constraint solver (LINCS).
Masses from `with_masses` weight the corrections.
An analytic SETTLE solves a rigid triangle such as three-site water.
Tolerances default to the rounding floor, and the coupling of each block sets the LINCS order and the iteration budgets.
A failure is a typed `ConstraintError` and leaves `x` as it was.
The C ABI (minor 31), the C++ wrapper and the xts aliases carry the set.
@@rst::doc:`howto/constraints`@@ shows how to use it, and @@rst::doc:`reference/constraints`@@ gives the equations.

A backtracking or Goldstein line search that runs out of trials now reports the step that produced the point it returns.
An L-BFGS session step that drops its own curvature pair now keeps the pair before it.

`minimize_scg`, `minimize_scg_exact` and `rgmin_minimize_scg` bound every trial step by a positive finite `Control::maxmove`, as that field documents.
Before, scaled conjugate gradient (SCG) ignored it.
The bound applies at the first trial and at each retry after a non-finite value.
Zero, negative, infinite and NaN values leave SCG unbounded.
Runs whose bound never binds give the same reports as before.
The comparison ratio of a bounded step divides by the damped model's change at that step, as in Nocedal and Wright eq. 4.4.
A short step therefore no longer halves the damping on an agreement as low as 0.375.
@@rst::doc:`explanation/step-bounds`@@ derives the ratio and sets out what can and cannot fix the size of a bound on log-hyperparameters.

A default `meson install` of rgmin as the top-level project installs `librgmin.so` into `libdir`.
`-Dwith_asv_helper=true` also builds and installs `librgmin_asv`, the timing helper that the asv suite loads.

`benchmarks/minimize.py` is an airspeed velocity (asv) suite that times one `rgmin_minimize` call on a convex quadratic in 16 and 64 dimensions.
`snakemake -c 1` calibrates an upper bound for each benchmark from repeated runs of `develop`.
`snakemake -c 1 pr_gate` exits non-zero when a benchmark is slower than that bound, and `benchflow/README.md` describes the workflow.

Under `Accept::None`, an L-BFGS trial on a curved kind that the box refuses returns `Error::OffManifold` instead of `Error::Oracle`.

On a curved manifold kind, a `fire2` session projects its secant velocity onto the tangent space at the new point.

On a curved manifold kind, Newton-CG and Newton-PCG retract their trust-region step, so every point the objective sees lies on the set.
CG runs on the model `P H P + (I - P)` for the tangent projection `P` of the kind, and flat kinds keep `x + p`.

On a curved manifold kind, a `Solver` step caps the tangent step and then retracts it, so every point it evaluates lies on the set.
On the unit sphere with a 0.1 cap, steepest descent, FIRE, FIRE 2.0 and dogleg evaluated points up to 1.1e-1 off it before.
Dogleg steps in the tangent space, and steepest descent and FIRE take one oracle call per step instead of two.
A trial that the box clip would move is refused before the oracle sees it, and a FIRE step with no trial left returns `Error::OffManifold`.
Flat kinds keep the old order and the old numbers.

`Solver::set_fire_preset` selects the FIRE 2.0 parameters of Guenole et al. 2020 Table 1 on a `fire2` session.
`Solver::set_fire_abc` turns on the accelerated bias-corrected (ABC) FIRE update of Echeverri Restrepo and Andric 2023, which ASE runs as `FIRE2(use_abc=True)`.
Both are opt-in, and @@rst::doc:`howto/fire`@@ shows them.
The C header `include/rgmin.h` declares `rgmin_solver_set_fire_preset` and `rgmin_solver_set_fire_abc`.
`abi_minor` 30.

`cargo cinstall` installs the hand-written `include/rgmin.h` and `dlpack/dlpack.h`.
The header compiles as C and as C++.
Version macros are `RGMIN_H_MAJOR`, `RGMIN_H_MINOR`, and `RGMIN_H_PATCH`.
`HighsInt` stays out of the public header.

How-to samples that did not compile now do.
The manifold sample defines its objective.
The HiGHS sample fills the rest of `HighsStep` from `Default`.
The intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) sample imports only what it uses.
The C++ sample calls `rgmin::minimize_fn` from `rgmin/optimize.hpp`.
The C samples include `rgmin.h`.

@@rst::doc:`Install rgmin <howto/install>`@@ shows how to install the 0.5.2 release from crates.io or the `develop` branch.
It gives the dependencies and features of each route, the C library through cargo-c, and the SciPy the HiGHS tests need.
The README, the index and the quickstart point to it.

The code of conduct, the security policy and the index name a contact, and the index links the issue tracker.

`examples/relax_morse.rs` is the program it runs.

Pull requests run the Org export and the Sphinx build.
The Pages deploy stays on a push to `main` or `workflow_dispatch`.

CI runs on pushes and pull requests to `develop` as well as `main`, and installs numpy and scipy for the HiGHS reference tests.

`Solver::set_stop_norm` selects the norm that every session stop test and `Report::grad_norm` use.
`StopNorm::Two` is the default.
`StopNorm::MaxAtom` is the largest per-atom norm (ASE `fmax`, eOn `max_atom`, LAMMPS `max`).
`StopNorm::Inf` is the largest absolute component (eOn `max_component`, LAMMPS `inf`).
`Report::grad` carries the gradient behind a session report.
C: `rgmin_solver_set_stop_norm` and `rgmin_solver_report_gradient`.
`abi_minor` 29.

The exponential preconditioner of Packwood et al., J. Chem. Phys. 144, 164109 (2016) ([10.1063/1.4947024](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4947024)) is `Solver::set_exp`.
The caller supplies the neighbour list.
L-BFGS uses `H0 = P^{-1}`.
FIRE and nonlinear CG use `P` as the metric.
A dense pair or Lindh matrix passed into the two-loop still wins.
C: `rgmin_exp_t`, `rgmin_solver_set_exp`, `rgmin_solver_clear_exp`, `rgmin_solver_exp_mu`.
The C++ session wraps those three as `set_exp`, `clear_exp`, and `exp_mu`.
`abi_minor` 28.

Capped Cartesian L-BFGS reserves the directional-curvature probe for a nominal step at least 64 times larger than the cap.
Ordinary starts use `H0 = 0.1 I` and five-value nonmonotone acceptance.
An installed exponential preconditioner replaces that scalar seed, including those steepest fallbacks.
Uncapped L-BFGS keeps the two-loop step and the Wolfe search.
A HiGHS feasible set and a non-Euclidean manifold stay on that path.

FIRE 2.0 follows Guénolé et al.'s semi-implicit update order, half-step-back uphill correction with a fresh corrected-point force, initial time-step delay, 2,000-step non-positive-power limit, and cap-consistent velocity.
An installed exponential preconditioner uses `P` as the metric: power is `F · v`, and the kick and the mix use `P^{-1} F`.

Newton and dogleg leave a first-order saddle.
When the force is already under `gtol`, the report reads the analytic Hessian.
The floor is max(abs(gtol), 1e-6, 1e-8 times the Frobenius norm of H).
A lowest eigenvalue below minus that floor steps along the mode, scaled to the per-atom cap, at most four times.
The dogleg radius restarts from the initial step.
A converged report costs one extra Hessian.

Steihaug-Toint Newton-CG is a session method: tokens `newton-cg` and `newton-pcg` (`RGMIN_NEWTON_CG` ` 24, ~RGMIN_NEWTON_PCG~ ` 25).
Hessian access is a product, analytic from `rgmin_solver_step_hvp` / `rgmin_minimize_hvp` and a one-gradient forward difference from `rgmin_solver_step`.
`maxmove` caps the Euclidean trust radius.
A per-atom cap clips the trial, and the boundary test uses the pre-clip length.
`rgmin_solver_gradient_calls` and `rgmin_solver_hvp_calls` count the two.
`rgmin_method_from_name` parses the token.
`abi_minor` 27.
Steihaug 1983 ([10.1137/0720042](https://doi.org/10.1137/0720042)); Nocedal and Wright, chapter 7.

`rgmin_solver_set_box`: per-coordinate HiGHS box on `x + p`.
A NULL side is unbounded.
Same status as `set_highs` (0, or 1 without the `highs` feature).
`rgmin_solver_set_trust` is the L_inf radius; `rgmin_solver_add_equality` / `rgmin_solver_clear_equalities` carry `a · p = rhs`.
`HighsStep.lo` / `hi` are per-coordinate vectors (length 1 is uniform).
`abi_minor` 22.

`xts.h` declares the exported `rgmin_minimize` / `rgmin_solver_*` symbols; `xts_minimize` and `xts_solver_*` are macro aliases.

Centered matrices (`centeredmatrix` / `RGMIN_MANIFOLD_CENTERED_MATRIX` = 22): manopt `centeredmatrixfactory`.
Packed row-major `m n`.
Projection is the centering operator (`X 1 = 0` by default, or `1^T X = 0`), retraction is `X + U` then center, transport is the identity.
Not the sphere and not a 3N cluster.
Tokens 7-10 stay reserved.
`abi_minor` 21.

Positive orthant (`positive` / `RGMIN_MANIFOLD_POSITIVE` = 21): manopt `positivefactory`.
Packed length `n`.
Projection is the identity, retraction is `x odot exp(v oslash x)`, transport is the identity.
Not the sphere and not a 3N cluster.
Tokens 7-10 stay reserved.
`abi_minor` 20.

Complex unit sphere (`spherecomplex` / `RGMIN_MANIFOLD_SPHERE_COMPLEX` = 20): manopt `spherecomplexfactory`.
Interleaved `(re, im)`, length `2 n`.
Projection is `v - Re(x^* v) x`, retraction is `(x+v)/||x+v||`, transport is projection at arrival.
Not the real sphere and not `(S^1)^n`.
Tokens 7-10 stay reserved.
`abi_minor` 19.

Symmetric doubly-stochastic matrices (`multinomialsymmetric` / `RGMIN_MANIFOLD_MULTINOMIAL_SYM` ` 19) and doubly-stochastic matrices (~multinomialdoublystochastic~ / ~RGMIN_MANIFOLD_MULTINOMIAL_DS~ ` 18): manopt `multinomialsymmetricfactory` and `multinomialdoublystochasticfactory`.
Both are packed row-major `n^2`, `n >= 2`, with Fisher projection and transport at arrival.
The retraction is Sinkhorn, and on the symmetric manifold it then symmetrizes.
A 3N cluster is rejected.
Tokens 7-10 stay reserved.
`abi_minor` 18 and 17.

Constant singleton (`constant` / `RGMIN_MANIFOLD_CONSTANT` = 17): manopt `constantfactory`.
Packed length `n`.
Projection and transport are the zero tangent, retraction is the fixed point.
A 3N cluster is rejected.
Tokens 7-10 stay reserved.
`abi_minor` 16.

Complex Euclidean (`euclidean_complex` / `RGMIN_MANIFOLD_EUCLIDEAN_COMPLEX` = 16): manopt `euclideancomplexfactory`.
Interleaved `(re, im)`, length `2 n`.
Projection is the identity, retraction is `x + v`, transport is the identity.
A 3N cluster is rejected.
Tokens 7-10 stay reserved.
`abi_minor` 15.

Skew-symmetric matrices (`skewsymmetric` / `RGMIN_MANIFOLD_SKEWSYMMETRIC` ` 15) and symmetric matrices (~symmetric~ / ~RGMIN_MANIFOLD_SYMMETRIC~ ` 14): manopt `skewsymmetricfactory` and `symmetricfactory`.
Both are packed row-major `n^2`, and the skew-symmetric one needs `n >= 2`.
Projection is `multiskew` (`0.5 (A - A^T)`) or symmetrization, retraction is `X + U`, transport is the identity.
A 3N cluster is rejected.
The symmetric manifold raised the ABI layout revision to 4.

L-BFGS session `Accept::None` takes the clipped two-loop direction.
Wolfe line search stays on Energy / Nonmonotone.

Scaled conjugate gradient (SCG) C waist: closed `xts_conjugacy_t` on `xts_scg_params_t` (FR`0 .. FrPr`7, dest leaf order).
`params==NULL` is Netlab Polak-Ribiere.

No Text.

## 0.2.0

`rgmin_solver_set_highs`: opt-in HiGHS feasible-set step.
With a host Hessian this is the convex Newton QP `min 1/2 p^T P p + g^T p` and per-coordinate boxes.
Without the `highs` feature the setter returns 1.
eindir / rgpot / eOn share the same session.

## 0.1.0

Rust rewrite of the C++ xtensor tree (`0.0.1` on the previous `main`).
Solvers live in Rust.
C and C++ reach them through the `rgmin_solver_t` session API and `rgmin_minimize` over dlpk tensors.

- Session API: `create` / `step` / `step_hess` / `step_fg` / fused `evalgrad` / `forget` / `free`.
- Methods: L-BFGS, BFGS, SR1, SR2, shifted Newton, rational function optimization (RFO), eight nonlinear conjugate gradient (NLCG) conjugacies, steepest, Adam, particle swarm optimization (PSO), FIRE, FIRE 2.0, Barzilai-Borwein, Powell dogleg.
- Host Hessian policy: `qn_step` two-loop / Newton / RFO; pair `H0 = P^{-1}`.
- Accept: none / energy / nonmonotone.
- Per-atom maxmove and optional rigid-body projection.
- Optional `highs` feature: two-loop direction, HiGHS only for a feasible set (box, trust, equalities).

The previous C++ `main` is unrelated history.
This tag is the first Rust release.

# Contributing

Report a bug or ask a question on the [issue tracker](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/issues).
Report a vulnerability as the [security policy](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/blob/develop/SECURITY.md) says, not in a public issue.
Everyone who takes part follows the [code of conduct](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/blob/develop/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), in issues and pull requests alike.

Pull requests go to the `develop` branch.
Commit subjects take the form `type(scope): summary`, as in `fix(session): report a stall when the energy test refuses a restart`.
A change that users can see adds a fragment to `docs/newsfragments/` and nowhere else.
The Unreleased sections of `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/orgmode/changelog.org` stay empty, so `towncrier build` does not list an entry twice.
The release commit copies the notes into the org page under a heading for the version.
`python3 scripts/check_changelog.py` fails when a fragment is paired with an Unreleased line.
Name the fragment `<issue>.<type>.md`, or `+<name>.<type>.md` for a change with no issue.
The type is `added`, `changed`, `deprecated`, `removed`, `fixed` or `security`, the sections of `CHANGELOG.md`.
Write it as one sentence per line, the way `CHANGELOG.md` reads.
`towncrier build` moves the fragments into `CHANGELOG.md` when a release is cut, with the settings in `towncrier.toml`.
To see the notes that the fragments give without changing a file:

```bash
python3 -m pip install towncrier
towncrier build --draft --version 0.0.0
```
## Build

Continuous integration (CI) runs these checks with Rust 1.88.0 on every push and pull request to `main` and `develop`.
Run them before you open a pull request.

```bash
rustup toolchain install 1.88.0 --profile minimal -c rustfmt
python3 -m pip install numpy scipy
cargo +1.88.0 fmt --all -- --check
cargo +1.88.0 test --locked
cargo +1.88.0 test --locked --features capi
cargo +1.88.0 test --locked --features highs
cargo +1.88.0 test --locked --features capi,highs
cargo +1.88.0 test --locked --features capi,par,highs,slepc,primme,chase,libkrylov
cargo +1.88.0 test --locked --features readcon
cargo +1.88.0 test --locked --features periodic-product
```
CI calls the fifth row all-features.
It names the features instead of passing `--all-features`, so the static library does not link `readcon-core` or the LGPL `gmp-mpfr-sys`, which get the last two rows.
When `capi` is also enabled the periodic-product module is omitted, so that build does not link GMP into the C static library. The periodic-product row is the one that builds the module, and it needs `m4`, `make`, `diffutils` and a C compiler.

The rows with `capi` also compile C and C++ programs against `include/` and run them.
Those tests run `cargo build --lib` for the target, profile and features of the test run and link the library it reports, so no `cargo build` has to come first.
They compile with `CC_<target>` and `CXX_<target>`, or `CC` and `CXX`, read the way the `cc` crate reads them.
Without those, they use the first of `cc`, `gcc` and `clang`, and of `c++`, `g++` and `clang++`, that builds a test program.
On Windows with MSVC they call `cl`, so run them from a Visual Studio developer prompt.
Under `--target` they default to the triple without its vendor and `-gcc` or `-g++`, such as `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc`, and run the programs through `CARGO_TARGET_<TRIPLE>_RUNNER` when it is set.
With or without `--target`, a command in `RGMIN_C_TEST_RUNNER`, such as `valgrind --error-exitcode=99`, runs the programs in place of that runner, as in the capi row of CI.

CI also runs clippy with warnings denied, on Rust 1.88.0 and on the latest stable, for the first five feature sets:

```

## Formulae

Nocedal-Wright equation numbers are the contract:

- NLCG is algorithm 5.4
- Inverse BFGS is 6.17
- L-BFGS two-loop is 7.4, scale is 7.20
- Strong Wolfe is 3.5 / 3.6
- Goldstein is 3.11
- Hager-Zhang beta is paper equation 1.3, not the C++ port

## Docs

Sphinx reads its reStructuredText export from `docs/source/`.
The docs workflow runs these steps, and you can run them from the top of the checkout:

(cd docs && emacs --batch -l export.el)
python3 docs/render_performance.py

```
Run the export inside `docs/`.
`export.el` reads `./orgmode/` and writes `./source/`, so run from anywhere else it writes nothing and still exits 0.
The export needs Org 9.7 or newer: ox-rst calls `org-element-type-p`, which that release added, and the Emacs on the docs runner comes with Org 9.6.
`export.el` installs a missing Org from the Emacs Lisp Package Archive (ELPA) of the GNU's Not Unix (GNU) project, and a missing ox-rst from Milkypostman's ELPA.
Its first run therefore needs network access.
It rewrites every page under `docs/source/`, including pages whose committed copy has drifted from the Org source.
Commit the export of the pages you edit, and leave the others out.

A `file:` link would point at the `.rst` file, which the built site does not have.

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/diis.org`

The step stores positions and gradients, oldest first, and drops
pairs past `memory`. The coefficients `c` solve

: min || sum_i c_i g_i ||    subject to sum_i c_i = 1

which is the bordered Gram system of Pulay, Chem. Phys. Lett. 73,
393 (1980). Wood and Zunger, J. Phys. A, 1343 (1985), name the
residual form. No DOI is attached for that line.

One stored pair, or a Gram matrix with no usable pivot, moves by
`-istep * g`. Two or more pairs move to `sum_i c_i x_i`. Neither
branch line searches on the oracle value, and neither applies a
kinetic preconditioner. `Control::maxmove` or
`Solver::set_atom_maxmove` caps the displacement the same way the
other direct steps do.

`Method::diis` keeps 6 pairs. The C selector is `RGMIN_DIIS` (22).
A control `memory` of 0 also means 6. ABI minor 30.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/ecnoise.org`

`ecnoise` reads `m + 1` values of one scalar function, with `m + 1 >= 4`,
and builds the forward-difference table. The default is `m = 8` (nine
samples). The level-`k` estimate is

: σ_k ` sqrt( γ_k * mean_i (Δ^k f_i)^2 ),    γ_k ` (k!)^2 / (2k)!

The returned noise is the smallest `k` whose column changes sign and
whose three estimates `σ_k`, `σ_{k+1}`, `σ_{k+2}` lie within a factor
of 4. Moré and Wild, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 33, 1292 (2011),
https://doi.org/10.1137/100786125.

`inform` 1 means that level was accepted. `inform` 2 means at least
half of the first differences are zero; the reference code retries at
`100 h`. `inform` 3 means the samples differ in the leading digit, or
no column meets the test; the reference code retries at `h / 100`.
A backend-declared value uses `inform` 0 and does not build the table.

`h` is the distance between consecutive samples, the spacing in the
`ECnoise.m` stencil `f(x - kh), ..., f(x + kh)`. It is not the
half-width of the stencil. `sample_noise` places
`x + (i - m/2) h u` for `i = 0, ..., m`, with `u` the unit vector
along the supplied direction.

The table does not supply a derivative. Its high differences are the
noise, of size `O(eps / h^k)`. `|f''|` and the third-derivative scale
`|T|` are separate central differences, Moré and Wild, ACM Trans.
Math. Softw. 38, 19 (2012), Algorithm 5.1,
https://doi.org/10.1145/2168773.2168777. The forward step and the
gradient probe that those scales imply are clamped to
`[max(1e-16, 4 ulp(max |x_i|)), 1]`.

Gradient noise is the table applied to `g(x + i h u) · w`. One unit
vector `w` is drawn from a counter keyed by `(seed, component)` and
is reused at every stencil point. The normal variate uses pure-Rust
`libm`, so the projection does not depend on the platform libm or on
the thread count. For any covariance `Σ`,
`E[(g · w)²] = tr(Σ) / n` because `w` is uniform on the sphere. The
Euclidean noise is `sqrt(n)` times that projection noise.

How to estimate the noise, choose the step, and stop on the floor is
[in the how-to](file:../howto/noise.org).

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/linesearch.org`

Every solver in this crate that follows a descent direction `d` from a
point `x` reduces the problem to one dimension. Write the restriction
of the objective along the ray as phi(a) = f(x + a d), so
phi'(0) = g . d is negative for any descent direction. The line
search's job is to pick a step `a` that provably makes progress
without spending the caller's evaluation budget, and every claim below
is about where those two guarantees come from.

# The two Wolfe conditions

Sufficient decrease (Armijo) demands phi(a) <= phi(0) + c1 a phi'(0)
with 0 < c1 < 1: the step must capture at least a `c1` fraction of the
decrease the initial slope promised. Because phi'(0) < 0 and a > 0,
the right-hand side sits strictly below phi(0), so an accepted point is
a real improvement, not a rounding story. That one-line consequence is
the Lean theorem `Rgmin.armijo_strict` in
[proofs/lean/Rgmin/Zoom.lean](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/blob/develop/proofs/lean/Rgmin/Zoom.lean).

The curvature condition demands abs(phi'(a)) <= c2 abs(phi'(0)) with
c1 < c2 < 1: the slope must have flattened enough that the quasi-Newton
update built from this step carries curvature information. Nocedal and
Wright's algorithms 3.5 and 3.6 (the bracket and the zoom) find a point
satisfying both.

Near a minimum the decrease test can fail on rounding alone. `Lbfgs::approx_wolfe`,
zero by default, is a fraction of abs(f) at the start of a strong Wolfe search.
A positive value accepts a trial inside that band when the strong curvature
test holds (Hager and Zhang 2005, stop T2) and places a trial inside the band
that fails the curvature test by the sign of its slope. The eOn cap does not
consult it. `LbfgsStep::Wolfe` and `Lbfgs::minimize_box` do. `src/linesearch/known.rs` implements them from a
point whose value and gradient the caller already holds: the start is
never re-evaluated, the accepted point comes back with its gradient,
and a displacement cap bounds every trial (`alpha_max`).
`src/linesearch/zoom.rs` keeps a standalone bisection zoom.

# The bracket and the zoom

The outer loop (`known.rs::wolfe`) expands a trial step, within
More-Thuente's bounds of 1.1 to 4 times the last increment, until it either
satisfies both conditions, overshoots (value above the Armijo line, or
above the previous trial), or the slope turns nonnegative. Overshoot
and slope-reversal both certify that a Wolfe point lies between the
last two trials: that pair becomes the bracket `[lo, hi]`, ordered so
`lo` carries the lower value.

The zoom then shrinks the bracket. Each iteration proposes a trial
inside `[lo, hi]`, evaluates it, and replaces whichever end the Wolfe
tests disqualify. The proposal is where the evaluation budget is won
or lost, and the guard is where termination is proved.

# The cubic Hermite proposal

At the two ends the zoom holds four numbers: phi(lo), phi'(lo),
phi(hi), phi'(hi). There is exactly one cubic through both points with
both slopes, and its interior minimizer has the closed form (Nocedal
and Wright eq. 3.59)

  d1 = phi'(lo) + phi'(hi) - 3 (phi(lo) - phi(hi)) / (lo - hi)
  d2 = sign(hi - lo) sqrt(d1^2 - phi'(lo) phi'(hi))
  t  = hi - (hi - lo) (phi'(hi) + d2 - d1) / (phi'(hi) - phi'(lo) + 2 d2)

On a well-behaved function the cubic model is third-order accurate, so
`t` lands close to the true minimizer and the zoom converges in a
handful of evaluations; the measured effect in anneal was 46 to 43
force calls per hop across the whole hopping battery, purely from this
proposal replacing bisection. When the discriminant goes negative or a
slope is non-finite the code falls back to the quadratic through
phi(lo), phi'(lo), phi(hi), and below that to bisection: the ladder
degrades in accuracy, never in safety.

# The guard is the termination proof

A cubic through awkward data can propose a point arbitrarily close to
either end, and a zoom that accepts such proposals can stall. The code
clamps every proposal into the middle eighty percent of the bracket:
no closer to an end than a tenth of the width. Two exact rational
facts follow, proved in
[Zoom.lean](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/blob/develop/proofs/lean/Rgmin/Zoom.lean):

- `Rgmin.guarded_above` / `Rgmin.guarded_below`: the clamp really does
  land in the interior band.
- `Rgmin.zoom_shrinks`: whichever end the trial replaces, the surviving
  bracket is at most `9/10` of the old width.

The width therefore decays geometrically (`Rgmin.width_envelope` is
the bound, `width_envelope_tendsto` takes it to zero in the limit),
and the evaluation budget of the zoom is logarithmic in the
requested tolerance regardless of what the cubic does. The Rust test
`the_cubic_zoom_keeps_the_evaluation_budget` in
`tests/lbfgs_state.rs` holds the crate to that budget on a quadratic
bowl.

# When rounding closes the bracket

Geometric contraction is not useful after floating-point arithmetic
can no longer distinguish the bracket. Following the relative-width
warning in More and Thuente's `dcsrch`
([10.1145/192115.192132](https://doi.org/10.1145/192115.192132)), Wolfe zoom stops when either the bracket
width is at most eight machine epsilons times its endpoint scale or a
sequence of eight trial values differ from the Armijo endpoint by
at most eight epsilons times
`max(abs(f_trial), abs(f_lo))` while Armijo fails. One unresolved
trial is not enough: an ordinary Wolfe search can cross a short run of
rounded values before finding curvature. A trial derivative that
crosses zero and grows past thirty-two times the initial descent slope
also keeps the bracket active; its sharp transition still carries
resolvable information. The named factors allow endpoint arithmetic
and one subtraction to round.

The reusable line search and the dedicated strict `Lbfgs::minimize`
Wolfe loop both wait for the sequence and honor the slope crossing:
callers may have non-smooth objectives, and a narrow basin can sit
past a run of rounded values. When the L-BFGS loop does stop, it keeps
its pairs instead of letting its fallback discard them and repeat a
full search from steepest descent. An explicit approximate-Wolfe
accuracy window remains the acceptance policy and does not take this
strict-value stop.

The search returns the lowest measured Armijo decrease, when one
exists, together with `LineSearchStopReason::RoundingBlocked`. If no
trial has a resolved decrease, the start remains the answer. An
L-BFGS session reports `StopReason::LineSearchRounding` and ends there;
it does not discard the curvature pairs and spend another Wolfe
budget along steepest descent. The rule depends only on the
one-dimensional step, value, and slope, so the line-search API remains
independent of the objective's physical system.

# When the interpolant is not used

The cubic and the quadratic model the objective on the bracket
$[\ell, h]$ from $\varphi(\ell)$, $\varphi'(\ell)$, $\varphi(h)$ and
$\varphi'(h)$. They carry information about the minimizer only when
$\varphi(h)$ is on the scale of the data at $\ell$. The zoom
interpolates when

$$|\varphi(h) - \varphi(\ell)| \le 10^3 \left(1 + |\varphi(\ell)| + |\varphi'(\ell)|\,(h - \ell)\right),$$

with $\varphi(h)$ finite, and takes the midpoint otherwise. The right
side adds the value magnitude to the change a model with unit
curvature predicts from the slope over the bracket; the factor
$10^3$ admits curvature three orders above that. A first trial worth
$4\cdot 10^{45}$ against $\varphi(\ell) = -24.6$ and
$\varphi'(\ell) \approx -5\cdot 10^3$ fails the test by forty
orders, and the fit through it returns the clamp of the bracket
rather than a point chosen by the objective. Bisection halves the
bracket until the values become comparable, after which the
interpolant resumes.

# What the accept layer adds

Above the line search, `src/accept.rs` offers three policies: take the
clipped step (one oracle call), refuse any energy rise (`Accept::Energy`,
up to ten halvings), or the Grippo-Lampariello-Lucidi nonmonotone
window. The fallback steepest-descent probe inside the energy policies
faces the same energy test as the step it replaces: a fallback that
also fails reports the position unmoved, and the caller's stall
machinery owns what happens next. The test
`accept_energy_uphill_does_not_take_ten_steepest_retries` pins the
oracle count of that path.

# A search the caller evaluates

`SuppliedSearch` takes the energy and gradient the caller already
holds. `offer` either names the next trial or returns the accepted
step. It does not call an objective, so a host that counts its own
evaluations (the C entry `rgmin_linesearch`, the Python class
`rgmin.LineSearch`) does not gain a second call inside
`rgmin_solver_step`. The trials are the ones `LineSearch::search`
makes on the same answers. `examples/tutorial_linesearch.rs` is that
comparison, and `tests/supplied_linesearch.rs` checks Wolfe,
backtracking, Goldstein and Brent one trial at a time.

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/precon.org`

# Exp, Lindh, and the bonded metric

Three sparse symmetric positive definite matrices share one solve and
one rebuild rule. The solve is Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate
gradients. The matrix is held until the largest atomic move exceeds
half the nearest-neighbour distance.

## Exp

Packwood, Kermode, Mones, Bernstein, Woolley, Gould, Ortner, and
Csányi, J. Chem. Phys. 144, 164109 (2016),
https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4947024.

The caller supplies the neighbour list. The weight on a pair is
`exp(-A (r / r_nn - 1))` with `A = 3`. Off-diagonal blocks are
`-μ c_ij I_3`. The diagonal is `μ (C_stab + sum_j c_ij) I_3` with
`C_stab = 0.1`. `r_nn` is the largest per-atom nearest-neighbour
distance. `μ` is the Rayleigh quotient of a sine probe against this
matrix at `μ = 1`. The probe's shifted gradient is an extra force
evaluation and is counted with the other force calls. ASE's
`estimate_mu` replaces a value below 1 with 1. rgmin keeps the
quotient. That cap is in eV/Å², so it is not invariant under a
change of energy or length unit. The pair weight and the sine probe
use one portable libm, so those bits match on x86_64 and aarch64.

## Lindh

Lindh, Bernhardsson, Karlström, and Malmqvist, Chem. Phys. Lett. 241,
423 (1995), https://doi.org/10.1016/0009-2614(95)00646-L.

The weights come from the paper's element tables for H, B, C, N, O, F,
Si, P, S, and Cl. A metal or a noble gas is not in those tables. Pairs
inside the cutoff come from a cell list: bins in lexicographic order,
then the pairs sorted by atom index, so the matrix does not depend on
the thread count.

## Bonded metric

Makri, Ortner, and Kermode, J. Chem. Phys. 150, 094109 (2019),
https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5064465, when the curvatures are that
field's. The matrix is the reduced (absolute-curvature) Hessian, which
matches ASE `FF` with `hessian='reduced'`. ASE's default is
`spectral`. `bonded_terms` with caller-supplied constants is the same
matrix and is a bonded geometric metric until those constants are the
field's. Harmonic bonds and angles, Morse bonds, and harmonic torsions
are the Rust terms. The C struct carries the harmonic bonds and angles.
Morse and the FF torsion stay in Rust. The Lindh torsion is a separate
flag.

## Which one

`select_precon` reads the geometry, the atomic numbers, and the
optimiser. `RGMIN_PRECON_AUTO` uses the session's own method, so C
does not pass the family.

| optimizer | geometry | atoms | elements | field | choice |
|---+---|---:|---|---|---|
| FIRE | any | any | any | any | identity |
| L-BFGS, CG | bulk, surface | >= 100 | any | ignored | Exp |
| L-BFGS, CG | bulk, surface | < 100 | any | ignored | identity |
| L-BFGS, CG | molecule, cluster | <= N_LINDH | Lindh set | no | Lindh |
| L-BFGS, CG | molecule, cluster | > N_LINDH | Lindh set | no | Exp at >= 100, else identity |
| L-BFGS, CG | molecule, cluster | any | Lindh set | yes | bonded metric |
| L-BFGS, CG | molecule, cluster | >= 100 | metal or noble gas | ignored | Exp |
| L-BFGS, CG | molecule, cluster | < 100 | metal or noble gas | ignored | identity |

The 100-atom line is ASE's `PreconLBFGS` rule. The bench has no bulk
below 100 atoms and no Cu147. The copper vacancy, 2047 atoms, is the
bulk row that uses Exp (L-BFGS 16 calls with none, 11 with Exp).
Water is the Lindh molecule (L-BFGS 5 calls, the same as none). Ar38
and Pt7 are the identity clusters. Lindh on lj38 ends at −164.88
against −167.77. The bonded metric on pt7 takes 18, 29, and 78 calls
against 10, 18, and 49, and on lj38 it ends at −166.65, so the field
is taken only for the covalent set.

`N_LINDH` is 2,000. On bulk diamond Si with a 4 Å cutoff the Jacobi
PCG iteration counts are Lindh 69, 124, 140 and Exp 21, 48, 85 at
160, 2,000, and 32,000 atoms. Eight solves on one thread take Lindh
0.031 s, 0.914 s, and 34.9 s against Exp 0.001 s, 0.031 s, and 1.03 s.
The iteration count levels off near 140, and 2,000 atoms is the
largest measured size at which eight Lindh solves still finish in
about a second.

Each kernel has its own atom-count gate, measured as the smallest
size where two threads beat one by more than the run-to-run range.
Lindh apply and Lindh solve gate at 2,000 atoms. Exp apply and Exp
solve gate at 32,000 atoms (at 8,000 atoms the Exp gaps, 0.67 ms and
0.015 s, sit inside ranges of 0.96 ms and 0.059 s). Assembly stays
serial: at 100,000 atoms the Exp gap is 0.026 s inside a range of
0.027 s. The gate does not read the thread count, so the result is
the same at 1, 2, 3, and 8 threads. Peak RSS at 100,000 atoms is
2.65 GB.

## H0 and the metric

L-BFGS multiplies its compact Hessian approximation by an initial
scale. Installing `P` sets that scale to `P^{-1}`, which is one
application of the solve. The two-loop recurrence then runs in the
Euclidean pair inner product, started from a Newton step in `P`.

Nonlinear CG and FIRE need the inner product that defines conjugacy
and the velocity mix. Both use `P` itself: the search direction is
`-P^{-1} g`, and the FIRE velocity is mixed with that direction. The
same `μ` that scales `P` scales the direction, so the first trial step
along it is order 1. Opening the line search at the control step
(0.01 in the bench) spends several extrapolations climbing back to
that step. The opening trial is Nocedal-Wright equation 3.60, and 1
on the first iteration when a metric is installed. A rebuilt `P`
restarts the recurrence at steepest descent because the stored
`P^{-1} g` was formed with the old matrix.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/product-manifold.org`

A point of a product manifold \(\mathcal{M} ` \mathcal{M}_1 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{M}_k\) is a tuple \(x ` (x_1, \dots, x_k)\) of factor points.
`ProductManifold` (`src/manifold/product.rs`) packs the tuple end to end in one vector and gives it the metric \(g = \sum_i w_i\, g_i\) with constant weights \(w_i > 0\).
This page derives every operation the solvers call from that one choice, shows where the weights enter and where they cancel, and compares the result with the products of manopt, Manifolds.jl, pymanopt and geomstats.
The first consumer is the optimal dividing hyperplane of transition-state theory in `rgsaddle`: a point and a unit normal in \(\mathbb{R}^n \times S^{n-1}\), or a unit normal and a signed offset in \(S(U) \times \mathbb{R}\), with \(U\) the directions a sampler moves in.
Later sections derive what that design needs beyond the product: the sphere of a subspace, metrics supplied on a factor's tangent spaces, gauge moves between steps and the convention for sphere Hessians.
The section on the optimal dividing plane puts them together; nothing else is specific to it.
@@rst::doc:`../reference/product-manifold`@@ lists the API.

Each factor \(\mathcal{M}_i\) sits in the space \(\mathcal{E}_i = \mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) of its packed coordinates, with tangent projector \(P_i(x_i)\) and metric \(g_i\).
For most kinds \(g_i\) is the Euclidean inner product of \(\mathcal{E}_i\) restricted to tangent vectors, which makes \(\mathcal{M}_i\) a Riemannian submanifold of \(\mathcal{E}_i\).
`Positive` and the doubly stochastic multinomials carry their own \(g_i\), through `Manifold::inner` and `Manifold::egrad2rgrad`.
A caller supplies \(\bar f\), the objective on the packed coordinates, with its coordinate gradient \(\nabla \bar f = (\nabla_1 \bar f, \dots, \nabla_k \bar f)\) and its Hessian action \(\nabla^2 \bar f\, u\).
The function optimized is the restriction \(f = \bar f|_{\mathcal{M}}\).

# Why a product, and why weights

A dividing hyperplane in mass-weighted coordinates \(y ` M^{1/2} r\) is \(\{y : n^\top (y - p) ` 0\}\), named by a point \(p \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and a unit normal \(n \in S^{n-1}\).
The pair \((p, n)\) lives on \(\mathbb{R}^n \times S^{n-1}\), a flat factor times a curved one.
Both factors are already kinds of `ManifoldKind`; what has to be derived is their product.

The plain product metric \(|\delta p|^2 + |\delta n|^2\) adds a squared mass-weighted length to a pure number.
Its value depends on the unit of length: going from ångström to bohr multiplies the first term by \(c^2\), with \(c \approx 1.89\), and leaves the second alone.
Every step length, trust radius, secant pair and stopping test measured with it inherits that dependence, so the path of the optimizer changes with the unit system.

Weights make that hidden parameter explicit.
Move the plane by \((\delta p, \delta n)\), with \(n^\top \delta n = 0\).
A point \(y = p + r e\) of the plane, \(e \perp n\) a unit vector, is displaced along the normal by
\[
(n + \delta n)^\top (y - p - \delta p) = r\, e^\top \delta n - n^\top \delta p + O(|\delta|^2).
\]
The shift moves every point of the plane by at most \(|\delta p|\), and the turn moves points at distance \(r\) by up to \(r |\delta n|\).
If the objective feels the plane out to a distance \(\ell\), in the units of \(p\), the two are comparable when \(|\delta p| \approx \ell |\delta n|\), and the natural size of a step is
\[
\|(\delta p, \delta n)\|^2 ` \ell^{-2} |\delta p|^2 + |\delta n|^2, \qquad w_p ` \ell^{-2}, \quad w_n = 1.
\]
Two scales are natural.
The geometric one is the mass-weighted radius of gyration of the system about \(p\).
The kinetic one uses that mass-weighted coordinates make the kinetic energy \(\tfrac12 |\dot y|^2\): an in-plane mode of angular frequency \(\omega\) at temperature \(T\) spreads over \(\ell = \sqrt{k_B T} / \omega\), again in the units of \(p\).
Either way \(\ell\) scales with the unit of length, so \(w_p\) carries the unit and the metric does not.
The section on the metric chart turns this into a statement about iterates.

The parameterization is redundant: \(p\) can slide inside the plane, and \((p, -n)\) names the same plane.
An objective that depends on the plane alone is constant along the in-plane part of \(\delta p\), so its Hessian is singular there.
Trust-region and quasi-Newton steps tolerate that.
A caller that wants a minimal parameterization writes \(p = s\, n\) and optimizes over \(\mathbb{R} \times S^{n-1}\).

# The product metric

For tangent vectors \(u = (u_1, \dots, u_k)\) and \(v\) at \(x\),
\[
g_x(u, v) ` \sum_{i`1}^k w_i\, g_{i, x_i}(u_i, v_i), \qquad w_i > 0.
\]
The tangent space is the direct sum \(T_x \mathcal{M} = T_{x_1} \mathcal{M}_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus T_{x_k} \mathcal{M}_k\) (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, section 3.1.6; Boumal, equation 3.31) @@rst::cite:`absilOptimizationAlgorithmsMatrix2008,boumalIntroductionOptimizationSmooth2023`@@, and \(g\) makes the blocks orthogonal.
At \(w_i = 1\) this is the product metric of Boumal, Example 3.57.
`ProductManifold::inner` is the weighted sum and `norm` its square root.

The weighted product of the \((\mathcal{M}_i, g_i)\) is the plain product of the scaled factors \((\mathcal{M}_i, w_i g_i)\).
Every fact about plain Riemannian products (Boumal, Table 7.2) therefore applies to it.
What remains is how the objects of one factor change when its metric is multiplied by a constant \(w > 0\):

| Object                                                          | Under \(g \mapsto w\, g\)                 |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------|
| Levi-Civita connection, geodesics, exponential, logarithm       | unchanged                                 |
| parallel transport                                              | unchanged                                 |
| retraction, vector transport                                    | unchanged; they do not involve the metric |
| inner product                                                   | times \(w\)                               |
| norm, distance, injectivity radius                              | times \(\sqrt{w}\)                        |
| gradient, Hessian operator, sectional curvature                 | times \(1 / w\)                           |

The Koszul formula,
\[
2 g(\nabla_X Y, Z) = X g(Y, Z) + Y g(X, Z) - Z g(X, Y) + g([X, Y], Z) - g([X, Z], Y) - g([Y, Z], X),
\]
is linear in \(g\) on both sides, so a constant factor leaves the connection unchanged, and with it geodesics, the exponential, the logarithm and parallel transport.
Lengths of curves scale by \(\sqrt{w}\), and so do distances and the injectivity radius.
The gradient solves \(w\, g(\mathrm{grad}_w f, u) ` \mathrm{D} f[u]\), so \(\mathrm{grad}_w f ` w^{-1} \mathrm{grad} f\), and the Hessian \(\nabla_u \mathrm{grad}_w f\) uses the same connection.
The curvature tensor depends on the connection alone, so the sectional curvature \(\langle R(u, v) v, u \rangle / (\|u\|^2 \|v\|^2 - \langle u, v \rangle^2)\) gains \(w\) above and \(w^2\) below.
geomstats' `ScalarProductMetric` rescales the methods of a metric by exactly these rules.

# The gradient

The Riemannian gradient is the tangent vector that represents the differential in the metric (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, section 3.6): \(g_x(\mathrm{grad} f(x), u) = \mathrm{D} f(x)[u]\) for every \(u \in T_x \mathcal{M}\).
Write \(\mathrm{D} f(x)[u] = \sum_i \mathrm{D}_i f(x)[u_i]\), with \(\mathrm{D}_i f\) the differential in the \(i\)-th argument, and let \(\mathrm{grad}_i f(x) \in T_{x_i} \mathcal{M}_i\) represent \(\mathrm{D}_i f(x)\) in \(g_i\).
Then
\[
\mathrm{grad} f(x) = \bigl( w_1^{-1} \mathrm{grad}_1 f(x), \dots, w_k^{-1} \mathrm{grad}_k f(x) \bigr),
\]
because
\[
g_x(\mathrm{grad} f(x), u) ` \sum_i w_i\, g_i\bigl(w_i^{-1} \mathrm{grad}_i f(x), u_i\bigr) ` \sum_i \mathrm{D}_i f(x)[u_i] = \mathrm{D} f(x)[u],
\]
and the representer is unique because \(g_x\) is nondegenerate.
At unit weights this is Boumal, Exercise 3.67.
A heavy factor gets a short gradient: its coordinates are expensive in the metric, so steepest descent moves them less.

# Projection and egrad2rgrad

When every \(g_i\) is induced by \(\mathcal{E}_i\), \(g\) is induced by the weighted inner product
\[
\langle a, b \rangle_W ` \sum_i w_i\, a_i^\top b_i ` a^\top W b, \qquad W = \mathrm{diag}(w_1 I_{n_1}, \dots, w_k I_{n_k}),
\]
on \(\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{E}_1 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{E}_k\), and \((\mathcal{M}, g)\) is a Riemannian submanifold of the Euclidean space \((\mathcal{E}, \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_W)\).
Two facts follow.

The \(W\)-orthogonal projector onto \(T_x \mathcal{M}\) is \(P(x) = \mathrm{diag}(P_1(x_1), \dots, P_k(x_k))\), free of weights.
The normal space of the product is the product of the factor normal spaces, and a vector normal to \(T_{x_i} \mathcal{M}_i\) in \(\mathcal{E}_i\) stays \(W\)-normal because \(W\) acts on block \(i\) as the scalar \(w_i\).
`ProductManifold::project` applies the factor projections block by block.

The \(W\)-gradient of \(\bar f\) is \(\nabla_W \bar f ` W^{-1} \nabla \bar f\), since \(\langle W^{-1} \nabla \bar f, b \rangle_W ` \nabla \bar f^\top b\) for every \(b\).
On a Riemannian submanifold the Riemannian gradient is the projected ambient gradient (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, section 3.6), so
\[
\mathrm{grad} f(x) ` P(x)\, W^{-1} \nabla \bar f(x) ` \bigl( w_i^{-1} P_i(x_i) \nabla_i \bar f(x) \bigr)_i,
\]
the gradient of the previous section with \(\mathrm{grad}_i f = P_i \nabla_i \bar f\).
A factor with its own metric enters the same way through its own `egrad2rgrad`, because the Riesz argument holds for any \(g_i\).
`ProductManifold::egrad2rgrad` applies each factor's `egrad2rgrad` to its block of \(\nabla \bar f\) and divides by \(w_i\).
Of the two maps a caller's gradient passes through, the projection and the gradient conversion, only the second sees the weights.

# The product retraction

A retraction is a smooth map \(R : T \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{M}\) with \(R_x(0_x) ` x\) and \(\mathrm{D} R_x(0_x) ` \mathrm{id}_{T_x \mathcal{M}}\) (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, Definition 4.1.1; Boumal, Definition 3.47).
The product retraction applies each factor's retraction to its block (Boumal, Exercise 3.50):
\[
R_x(v) = \bigl( R^{(1)}_{x_1}(v_1), \dots, R^{(k)}_{x_k}(v_k) \bigr).
\]

/First-order agreement./
Each block is smooth in \((x_i, v_i)\), so \(R\) is smooth on \(T \mathcal{M} ` T \mathcal{M}_1 \times \cdots \times T \mathcal{M}_k\), and \(R_x(0_x) ` (R^{(i)}_{x_i}(0))_i = x\).
For \(v \in T_x \mathcal{M}\) the curve \(c(t) ` R_x(t v)\) has the blocks \(c_i(t) ` R^{(i)}_{x_i}(t v_i)\), so
\[
c'(0) ` \bigl( \mathrm{D} R^{(i)}_{x_i}(0)[v_i] \bigr)_i ` (v_i)_i = v.
\]
Hence \(\mathrm{D} R_x(0_x) ` \mathrm{id}\), and in the packed coordinates \(R_x(t v) ` x + t v + O(t^2)\): the retraction agrees with the step to first order.
The weights appear nowhere, since neither condition involves the metric.

A retraction is second order when its curves also start with zero covariant acceleration, \(\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{d}t} c'(0) = 0\) (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, equation 5.33; Boumal, Definition 5.42).
The connection of a product is the product of the factor connections (Boumal, Exercises 5.4 and 5.13), and the weights do not change it, so the acceleration of \(c\) is the tuple of the factor accelerations.
The product retraction is therefore second order exactly when every factor retraction is.
The straight line of a flat factor and the normalized step on the sphere (Boumal, Example 5.43) are second order; the QR retraction of SO(3) is first order only.
The local rate of the trust region does not need a second-order retraction (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, Proposition 5.5.6), but the numerical Hessian check does (Boumal, section 6.8).
That is why the tests run the check along the exponential wherever a retraction is first order.

# Exponential, logarithm, distance and injectivity radius

Geodesics of the product are tuples of factor geodesics (Boumal, Exercise 5.39), and the weights leave them alone, so (Boumal, Exercise 10.32)
\[
\exp_x(v) ` \bigl( \exp_{x_i}(v_i) \bigr)_i, \qquad \log_x(y) ` \bigl( \log_{x_i}(y_i) \bigr)_i.
\]
If \(\exp_x(v) ` y\) then \(\exp_{x_i}(v_i) ` y_i\) for every \(i\), and \(\|v\|_x^2 = \sum_i w_i \|v_i\|_{x_i}^2\) is smallest when every block is.
So, where each factor logarithm is defined, the tuple of factor logarithms is the logarithm of the product for every choice of positive weights.
The distance follows from Boumal, Exercise 10.14, applied to the scaled factors:
\[
\mathrm{dist}(x, y) = \Bigl( \sum_i w_i\, \mathrm{dist}_i(x_i, y_i)^2 \Bigr)^{1/2}.
\]

The exponential at \(x\) is a diffeomorphism on the \(g\)-ball of radius \(r\) exactly when every factor exponential is one on its \(w_i g_i\)-ball of radius \(r\).
A vector supported on one block shows that the condition is necessary.
It is sufficient because the \(g\)-ball lies inside the product of the factor balls, where the exponential is a product of diffeomorphisms.
So
\[
\mathrm{inj}(x) = \min_i \sqrt{w_i}\, \mathrm{inj}_i(x_i),
\]
and a flat factor, with \(\mathrm{inj}_i = \infty\), does not constrain it.
A 2-plane tangent to factor \(i\) has sectional curvature \(K_i / w_i\), and a plane spanned by vectors from two different factors has curvature zero.
For \(k \ge 2\) the curvature bounds are \(\min(0, \min_i K_i^{\min} / w_i)\) and \(\max(0, \max_i K_i^{\max} / w_i)\).
`Manifold` has no injectivity or curvature hook; the two formulas are stated for step-size arguments and for the comparison below.

`ProductManifold::exp` and `log` return `None` as soon as one factor has no closed form.
`dist` is the weighted root sum of squares.

# Vector transport

A vector transport with associated retraction \(R\) maps \(\xi \in T_x \mathcal{M}\) along \(\eta \in T_x \mathcal{M}\) to \(\mathcal{T}_\eta \xi \in T_{R_x(\eta)} \mathcal{M}\), with \(\mathcal{T}_{0_x} \xi = \xi\) and \(\mathcal{T}_\eta\) linear (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, Definition 8.1.1).
The blockwise transport
\[
\mathcal{T}_\eta \xi = \bigl( \mathcal{T}^{(i)}_{\eta_i} \xi_i \bigr)_i
\]
satisfies the three conditions because each block does.
It lands in \(\bigoplus_i T_{R_{x_i}(\eta_i)} \mathcal{M}_i ` T_{R_x(\eta)} \mathcal{M}\), it is the identity at \(\eta ` 0\), and it is linear.
Its associated retraction is the product retraction, and it does not involve the metric.
For a Riemannian submanifold factor `transport` is projection onto the arrival tangent space (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, section 8.1.3), so on a product of them it is \(P(y)\), the \(W\)-orthogonal projection.

The product transport is an isometry of \(g\) exactly when every factor transport is an isometry of its \(g_i\).
If each is, then
\[
g_y(\mathcal{T} \xi, \mathcal{T} \zeta) ` \sum_i w_i\, g_i(\mathcal{T}^{(i)} \xi_i, \mathcal{T}^{(i)} \zeta_i) ` \sum_i w_i\, g_i(\xi_i, \zeta_i) = g_x(\xi, \zeta).
\]
If one is not, vectors supported on that block break the identity.
The weights can neither repair nor break isometry, so `transport_is_isometric` is the conjunction over the factors.
Projection is an isometry only where neither the tangent space nor the metric changes: Euclidean space and the linear subspaces.
On \(\mathbb{R}^n \times S^{n-1}\) it is not.

# Parallel transport and the locking condition

Parallel transport along a curve \(c = (c_1, \dots, c_k)\) is the tuple of factor parallel transports (Boumal, Exercise 10.39), unchanged by the weights because the connection is.
It is an isometry of \(g\): each block is an isometry of \(g_i\), and so of \(w_i g_i\).
`parallel_transport_along(x, d, v)` carries \(v\) along \(t \mapsto \exp_x(t d)\) from \(t ` 0\) to \(t ` 1\), and `parallel_transport(x, y, v)` takes \(d = \log_x(y)\).

The Riemannian Broyden class of Huang, Gallivan and Absil ([SIAM J. Optim. 25, 1660 (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1137/140955483)) pairs a retraction \(R\) with an isometric transport \(\mathcal{T}_S\) under the locking condition
\[
\mathcal{T}_{S_\xi} \xi = \beta\, \mathcal{T}_{R_\xi} \xi, \qquad
\beta = \frac{\|\xi\|}{\|\mathcal{T}_{R_\xi} \xi\|}, \qquad
\mathcal{T}_{R_\xi} \xi ` \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} R_x(t \xi) \Big|_{t ` 1}.
\]
Take \(R = \exp\) and \(\mathcal{T}_S\) parallel transport along the geodesic.
The velocity of a geodesic is parallel along it, so \(\mathcal{T}_{R_\xi} \xi ` P_{0 \to 1} \xi\), its length is \(\|\xi\|\), \(\beta ` 1\), and the condition holds with equality.
On the product it holds block by block and so for the tuple, for every choice of weights.
A product whose factors all supply the exponential and parallel transport therefore carries a retraction and transport pair that meets the hypotheses of that theory.
The session's L-BFGS moves its pairs with `transport`, projection, and does not rely on them.

# The Riemannian Hessian and ehess2rhess

The Riemannian Hessian is \(\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u] = \nabla_u \mathrm{grad} f\) (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, Definition 5.5.1).
For a plain product, Boumal's Example 5.19 (equation 5.12, stated for two factors and extended to \(k\) by grouping) gives, with \(G_i = \mathrm{grad}_i f\),
\[
\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u]_i = \mathrm{Hess}_i f(x)[u_i] + \sum_{j \ne i} \mathrm{D}_j G_i(x)[u_j].
\]
The cross terms \(\mathrm{D}_j G_i\) couple the blocks; only the diagonal terms carry the curvature of the factors.
On the scaled factors \(G_i\) becomes \(w_i^{-1} G_i\) and \(\mathrm{Hess}_i\) becomes \(w_i^{-1} \mathrm{Hess}_i\), so for the weighted product
\[
\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u]_i = w_i^{-1} \Bigl( \mathrm{Hess}_i f(x)[u_i] + \sum_{j \ne i} \mathrm{D}_j G_i(x)[u_j] \Bigr).
\]

For Riemannian submanifold factors the weighted ambient space gives the same result with the Weingarten terms explicit.
On a Riemannian submanifold of a Euclidean space (Boumal, Corollary 5.47; Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, Proposition 5.3.2, for the connection it rests on),
\[
\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u] = P(x) \bigl( \nabla^2 \bar f(x)[u] \bigr) + \mathfrak{W}_x\bigl(u, P^\perp(x) \nabla \bar f(x)\bigr),
\]
where the Weingarten map \(\mathfrak{W}_x\) carries the curvature of the embedding.
In \((\mathcal{E}, \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_W)\) the ambient gradient is \(W^{-1} \nabla \bar f\) and the ambient Hessian is \(W^{-1} \nabla^2 \bar f\).
The projector is blockwise and free of weights, and so is the Weingarten map: the normal spaces and projectors of block \(i\) are those of \(\mathcal{M}_i \subset \mathcal{E}_i\), and \(W\) acts on the block as a scalar, so the defining identity of \(\mathfrak{W}_i\) holds with both sides multiplied by \(w_i\).
Block \(i\) of the Hessian is therefore
\[
\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u]_i
= w_i^{-1} \Bigl( P_i(x_i) \bigl( \nabla^2 \bar f(x)\, u \bigr)_i + \mathfrak{W}_i\bigl(u_i, P_i^\perp(x_i) \nabla_i \bar f(x)\bigr) \Bigr)
= w_i^{-1}\, \mathrm{ehess2rhess}_i\bigl(x_i, \nabla_i \bar f, (\nabla^2 \bar f\, u)_i, u_i\bigr).
\]
The block \((\nabla^2 \bar f\, u)_i = \sum_j \nabla^2_{ij} \bar f\, u_j\) of the caller's full Hessian action carries the cross terms; the factor adds only its own Weingarten term.
The same holds for every kind in the crate that supplies `ehess2rhess`, including those with their own metric.
Each such map is affine in the Hessian action with linear part the kind's `egrad2rgrad`, and \(\mathrm{D}_j G_i(x)[u_j] = \mathrm{egrad2rgrad}_i(\nabla^2_{ij} \bar f\, u_j)\), so the off-diagonal blocks of the action produce exactly the cross terms of equation 5.12.
`ProductManifold::ehess2rhess` applies each factor's map to its block of the full action and divides by \(w_i\).

For the hyperplane, with the sphere's Weingarten term \(\mathfrak{W}_n(u_n, \nu) = -(n^\top \nu)\, u_n\),
\[
\mathrm{Hess} f(p, n)[u]
= \Bigl( w_p^{-1} \bigl( \nabla^2 \bar f\, u \bigr)_p,\;
w_n^{-1} \bigl( (I - n n^\top) (\nabla^2 \bar f\, u)_n - (n^\top \nabla_n \bar f)\, u_n \bigr) \Bigr).
\]

The weights cancel in the bilinear form,
\[
g_x\bigl(\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u], v\bigr) = v^\top \nabla^2 \bar f(x)\, u + \sum_i \mathfrak{W}_i\bigl(u_i, P_i^\perp \nabla_i \bar f(x)\bigr)^\top v_i,
\]
which is symmetric in \(u\) and \(v\) because each Weingarten map is self-adjoint.
They cancel in the Newton equation too: \(\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[\eta] = -\mathrm{grad} f(x)\) has \(w_i^{-1}\) on both sides of block \(i\), so the Newton step does not depend on the weights.
Only the steps that measure, the gradient step and the trust region, see them.

# Typical distance and the trust-region defaults

manopt's `typicaldist` is the distance scale a trust region starts from.
If every factor moves by its own typical distance \(t_i\), the product moves by
\[
t(\mathcal{M}) = \Bigl( \sum_i w_i\, t_i^2 \Bigr)^{1/2},
\]
the weighted form of manopt's root sum of squares and the value of `ProductManifold::typical_dist`.
The factor values follow the manopt factories: \(\pi\) for a sphere, \(\pi \sqrt{3}\) for SO(3), \(\pi \sqrt{m}\) for \(m\) oblique columns and \(\sqrt{n}\) for \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

`rtr::minimize_rtr` is the trust region with truncated conjugate gradients of Absil, Baker and Gallivan ([Found. Comput. Math. 7, 303 (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-005-0179-9); Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, Algorithms 10 and 11).
It runs in the metric of the manifold: the gradient by `egrad2rgrad`, the Hessian by `ehess2rhess`, and every inner product, norm and the trust ball by `inner`.
`RtrOptions` takes the defaults of manopt `trustregions`:
- \(\bar\Delta\) the typical distance and \(\Delta_0 = \bar\Delta / 8\);
- acceptance above \(\rho' ` 0.1\), the radius quartered below \(\rho ` 1/4\) and doubled, up to \(\bar\Delta\), above \(\rho = 3/4\) on the boundary;
- the inner rule \(\|r_j\| \le \|r_0\| \min(\|r_0\|^\theta, \kappa)\) with \(\theta ` 1\) and \(\kappa ` 0.1\) (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, equation 7.10), and an inner budget of the packed length, which bounds the dimension;
- `rho_regularization` \(10^3\), which adds \(10^3 \varepsilon \max(1, |f|)\) to both decreases so that steps below the rounding of \(f\) read \(\rho \approx 1\).
With the exact Hessian the local rate is \(\min(\theta + 1, 2)\) (Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, Theorem 7.4.11), quadratic at \(\theta = 1\).
A factor without `ehess2rhess` makes the product fall back to `egrad2rgrad` of the ambient action, the Gauss-Newton part of the Hessian, which loses that rate.

The typical distance of a flat factor is the one place a unit enters again.
\(\pi\) is intrinsic to a sphere, but \(\sqrt{n}\) for \(\mathbb{R}^n\) counts coordinates in whatever unit they are written in.
Under \(p' ` c\, p\) and \(w_p' ` w_p / c^2\) the term \(w_p\, n\) becomes \(w_p\, n / c^2\), and the default \(\bar\Delta\) moves.
A run that must not depend on the unit sets \(\bar\Delta\) from a physical length with `RtrOptions::with_radius_max`, for instance \(\bar\Delta = (w_p L^2 + w_n \pi^2)^{1/2}\) with \(L\) the largest shift of \(p\) worth trusting.

# The metric chart and unit invariance

The session steppers, L-BFGS, conjugate gradients, FIRE, the Newton-CG trust region and the rest, measure steps, curvature pairs and gradients with the dot product of the packed vector.
On a weighted product that is not \(g\).
Rather than thread \(g\) through every stepper, a session stores a weighted product in the coordinates where \(g\) is the dot product.

The map \(\phi(x) ` (\sqrt{w_1}\, x_1, \dots, \sqrt{w_k}\, x_k)\) is a diffeomorphism from \(\mathcal{M}\) onto the product of the scaled sets \(\sqrt{w_i}\, \mathcal{M}_i\), with \(\mathrm{D} \phi(x)[u] ` (\sqrt{w_i}\, u_i)_i\).
For Riemannian submanifold factors
\[
\mathrm{D} \phi(x)[u]^\top \mathrm{D} \phi(x)[v] ` \sum_i w_i\, u_i^\top v_i ` g_x(u, v),
\]
so \(\phi\) is an isometry onto \(\prod_i \sqrt{w_i}\, \mathcal{M}_i\) with the Euclidean metric of the packed vector, and a stepper that measures with dot products in \(z = \phi(x)\) measures in \(g\).
`ProductManifold::chart` is that product and `ProductManifold::chart_scales` is \(d\), equal to \(\sqrt{w_i}\) on the coordinates of factor \(i\).
A block stores \(s_i x_i\) for a factor point \(x_i\) and carries the metric \(c_i\, g_i\), with \(c_i s_i^2 ` w_i\): \(s_i ` 1\) and \(c_i ` w_i\) in natural coordinates, \(s_i ` \sqrt{w_i}\) and \(c_i = 1\) in the chart.
Every operation divides the block by \(s_i\), calls the factor and scales back.
The Weingarten term of the scaled factor \(s_i \mathcal{M}_i\) is \(1 / s_i\) times the unit one, which the code obtains by passing the factor \(\nabla_i \bar f / s_i\).

`Solver::set_manifold` and `Solver::set_product` store a product whose weights are not all one as its chart.
The caller keeps natural coordinates: the session reads the objective as \(\tilde f(z) = \bar f(z \oslash d)\), so that
\[
\nabla_z \tilde f = \nabla_x \bar f \oslash d, \qquad
\nabla_z^2 \tilde f = D^{-1} \nabla_x^2 \bar f\, D^{-1}, \qquad
\nabla_z^2 \tilde f\, v = D^{-1} \nabla_x^2 \bar f\, (D^{-1} v),
\]
with \(D = \mathrm{diag}(d)\).
Box bounds are scaled by \(d\), and the point, the reported coordinates and the reported gradient are mapped back.
The reported gradient norm is already its \(g\)-length.
Factors with their own metric (`Positive`, the doubly stochastic multinomials) are stepped in the chart as a session steps them alone, with their Riemannian gradient and dot products.
`minimize_rtr` needs no chart, since it measures everything with `inner`.

Settings that read raw coordinates as atoms or boxes cannot be rescaled behind the caller's back, and a weighted product refuses them with `Error::ProductChart`.
They are the exponential preconditioner, the Lindh model Hessian, rigid-motion projection of the whole vector, and the HiGHS box and equalities.
Rigid factors (`MwRigid`, `RigidQuotient`) inside a product are projected block by block with the session's masses and periodic flag.
`MwRigid` blocks read the masses as one molecule reused on every block, or as the concatenation over the `MwRigid` blocks.

/Unit invariance./
Change the unit of a factor, \(x_i' ` c\, x_i\), and its weight with it, \(w_i' ` w_i / c^2\).
The chart coordinate does not change, \(\sqrt{w_i'}\, x_i' ` \sqrt{w_i}\, x_i\), and the objective written in the new unit, \(\bar f'(x') ` \bar f(x)\), reads in the chart as the same function \(\tilde f\).
A deterministic stepper started at the same chart point therefore produces the same chart iterates, and mapping back gives \(x_i' = c\, x_i\) at every step.
The iterates do not depend on the unit once the weight carries it; in floating point they agree to rounding.
The test `iterates_do_not_depend_on_the_length_unit_once_the_weight_carries_it` runs fifteen L-BFGS steps on the hyperplane in ångström with \(w_p\) and in bohr with \(w_p / c^2\), and finds them equal to \(10^{-9}\).
Keeping \(w_p\) in bohr moves them by more than \(10^{-4}\).
The same test runs `minimize_rtr` in both units with \(\bar\Delta\) set explicitly, and finds the same iteration count, accepted steps and minimizer.

# The sphere of a subspace

A sampler that fixes the centre of mass, or holds some atoms still, moves only in a linear subspace \(U \subset \mathbb{R}^n\), and the normal of a plane it samples must lie in \(U\) too.
The normal is then a point of the unit sphere of \(U\),
\[
S(U) ` \{ x \in U : \|x\| ` 1 \}.
\]
`SubspaceSphere` (`src/manifold/subspace_sphere.rs`) takes \(U\) as the span of the rows of a matrix, `SubspaceSphere::within`, or as the orthogonal complement of that span, `SubspaceSphere::excluding`.
The caller passes the smaller basis: the centre-of-mass directions and the coordinates of fixed atoms are excluded, a rotation subspace of a few modes is kept.
The rows are orthonormalized once into \(Q\), so that \(P_U\) is \(Q^\top Q\) or \(I - Q^\top Q\), applied in two passes over the rows rather than as a dense \(n \times n\) matrix.
`ManifoldKind::sphere_within` and `ManifoldKind::sphere_excluding` wrap the two constructors.

\(U\) with the Euclidean inner product is a Euclidean space, so \(S(U)\) is a sphere, a Riemannian submanifold of \(U\) and therefore of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
Its tangent space at \(x\) is \(\{v \in U : x^\top v = 0\}\).
Since \(P_U x = x\), the projectors \(P_U\) and \(x x^\top\) commute, and
\[
P_x ` (I - x x^\top) P_U ` P_U - x x^\top
\]
is symmetric and idempotent with range \(U \cap x^\perp\): it is the orthogonal projector onto the tangent space.
The Riemannian gradient is \(P_x \nabla \bar f = P_U \nabla \bar f - (x^\top \nabla \bar f)\, x\).

The retraction normalizes the step inside \(U\),
\[
R_x(v) = \frac{P_U (x + v)}{\|P_U (x + v)\|}.
\]
For \(x \in S(U)\) and a tangent \(v\) the projection changes nothing in exact arithmetic, so \(R_x(v)\) is the point of \(S(U)\) nearest to \(x + v\).
That is the metric projection retraction, which is second order (Boumal, Propositions 5.54 and 5.55, and Example 5.43 for the sphere).
In floating point the projection removes the rounding that would otherwise build up along the excluded directions over a long run.
Transport is projection onto the arrival tangent space.

For the Hessian, extend the gradient off the manifold by \(\bar G(y) = P_U \nabla \bar f(y) - (y^\top \nabla \bar f(y))\, y\).
Its differential is
\[
\mathrm{D} \bar G(x)[u] = P_U \nabla^2 \bar f(x)\, u - \bigl( u^\top \nabla \bar f(x) + x^\top \nabla^2 \bar f(x)\, u \bigr)\, x - (x^\top \nabla \bar f(x))\, u,
\]
and \(P_x\) removes \(x\), keeps a tangent \(u\) and satisfies \(P_x P_U = P_x\), so Boumal's Corollary 5.16 gives
\[
\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u] = P_x \bigl( \nabla^2 \bar f(x)\, u - (x^\top \nabla \bar f(x))\, u \bigr),
\]
the sphere's formula with \(P_x\) in place of \(I - x x^\top\).
\(U\) is flat, so the part of \(\nabla \bar f\) in \(U^\perp\) adds no curvature and only the radial part \(x^\top \nabla \bar f\) bends: the Weingarten map of \(S(U)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is \(\mathfrak{W}_x(u, \nu) = -(x^\top \nu)\, u\) for every normal \(\nu \in U^\perp \oplus \mathrm{span}(x)\).

\(S(U)\) is a great sphere of \(S^{n-1}\).
For \(x \in S(U)\) and a tangent \(v\), the great circle \(\cos(t \|v\|)\, x + \sin(t \|v\|)\, v / \|v\|\) stays in \(U\), and a geodesic of \(S^{n-1}\) that stays in a submanifold is a geodesic of the submanifold.
The exponential, logarithm, distance and parallel transport are therefore the sphere's, the injectivity radius is \(\pi\), and so is `typical_dist`.

Gram–Schmidt runs twice over the rows, which keeps them orthonormal to rounding even when they are nearly dependent.
After the two passes the residual of a row of length \(L\) carries an error of order \(\varepsilon L\), and normalizing a residual of length \(\rho\) leaves an error of order \(\varepsilon L / \rho\) in its orthogonality to the earlier rows.
A row whose residual is at most \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\, L\) would leave more than \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\), and is refused as dependent.
The constructors also refuse an ambient dimension of zero, an entry that is not finite, no kept direction and excluded directions that fill \(\mathbb{R}^n\), all with `Error::SubspaceBasis`.
A single kept direction \(u\) gives the two points \(\pm u\), at which every tangent vector is zero.

# Tangent metrics

A weight scales a whole factor.
At the optimal plane the rotation block of the harmonic free energy is \(k_B T (I + |\lambda_1| H_\parallel^{-1})\), whose eigenvalues follow the in-plane curvatures of the saddle across decades, and no single scalar matches them.
A `TangentMetric` supplies an operator \(G_x\) on the tangent spaces of one factor, self-adjoint and positive definite in \(g_i\) and smooth in \(x\), and that factor's part of the metric becomes
\[
w_i\, g_i(u, G_x v).
\]
`ProductFactor::with_metric` attaches one; `TangentMetric::apply` returns \(G_x v\) and `TangentMetric::solve` returns \(G_x^{-1} r\).
The product projects both results onto the tangent space, which removes rounding but does not repair an operator that leaves it.

/Gradient./
The Riesz condition \(w_i\, g_i(\mathrm{grad}_G f, G_x u) = \mathrm{D}_i f(x)[u]\) and the self-adjointness of \(G_x\) give
\[
\mathrm{grad}_G f = w_i^{-1} G_x^{-1}\, \mathrm{grad}_i f.
\]
`egrad2rgrad` therefore returns the preconditioned gradient, and a driver that steps along it, deterministic or sampled, is preconditioned without knowing it.

/Hessian model./
The Riemannian Hessian of the new metric needs its Levi-Civita connection, which involves derivatives of \(G_x\) in \(x\) that an operator supplied as `apply` and `solve` does not give.
`ehess2rhess` returns instead
\[
H_G[u] = w_i^{-1} G_x^{-1}\, \mathrm{Hess}_i f(x)[u],
\]
with \(\mathrm{Hess}_i\) the factor's Hessian in \(g_i\).
It has the three properties the trust region needs.
It is self-adjoint in the new metric, since \(w_i\, g_i(H_G u, G_x v) = g_i(\mathrm{Hess}_i f(x)[u], v)\).
It is exact at a critical point, where the Hessian depends on the metric only through the inner product on the tangent space (Boumal, Proposition 5.45 and the remark after it): there \(g_G(\mathrm{Hess}_G f(x)[u], v) ` g(\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u], v) ` g_G(H_G u, v)\).
Away from critical points the bilinear forms of two Riemannian Hessians of one function differ by \(\mathrm{D} f(x)[\Gamma_x(u, v)]\), with \(\Gamma\) the difference of the two Levi-Civita connections, and the Hessian of the pullback \(\hat f_x = f \circ R_x\) at \(0\) differs from either by another term linear in \(\mathrm{D} f(x)\).
\(H_G\) thus meets the condition \(\|H_k - \mathrm{Hess} \hat f_{x_k}(0)\| \le \beta_H \|\mathrm{grad} f(x_k)\|\) of Absil, Mahony and Sepulchre, Theorem 7.4.11, and `minimize_rtr` keeps its local rate \(\min(\theta + 1, 2)\) in the new metric.

/Preconditioned truncated CG./
In this metric the truncated conjugate gradients of `minimize_rtr` are manopt's preconditioned `trs_tCG` in the unweighted metric \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\), with the preconditioner \(P\) equal to \((w_i G_x)^{-1}\) on block \(i\).
The residual of the model in the new metric is \(P r\), with \(r\) the residual in the unweighted metric.
The step length \(\langle P r, P r \rangle_G / \langle \delta, H_G \delta \rangle_G ` \langle r, P r \rangle / \langle \delta, \mathrm{Hess} f\, \delta \rangle\) is manopt's ~z_r / d_Hd~, and the trust ball \(\|\eta\|_G^2 ` \langle \eta, P^{-1} \eta \rangle \le \Delta^2\) is manopt's, so the iterates are the same.
Two tests differ.
The inner rule here reads the residual in the new metric, \(\langle r, P r \rangle^{1/2}\), where manopt reads \(\|r\|\); manopt's source calls the choice arbitrary and notes that Conn, Gould and Toint accept both (@@rst::cite:`connTrustRegionMethods2000`@@, page 206).
The outer test here reads \(\|\mathrm{grad}_G f\|_G = \langle \mathrm{grad} f, P\, \mathrm{grad} f \rangle^{1/2}\), where manopt reads \(\|\mathrm{grad} f\|\).

/What the metric costs./
The geodesics of the new metric have no closed form, so the exponential, logarithm, distance and both parallel transports of a product with a tangent metric return `None`.
Projection is not an isometry of the new metric, so `transport_is_isometric` is false.
`typical_dist` ignores \(G\), which has no single scale; a caller whose \(G\) changes lengths by much sets \(\bar\Delta\) with `RtrOptions::with_radius_max`.

/Nesting, the chart and sessions./
A factor that is itself a product takes tangent metrics on its own factors, and flattening keeps them.
A metric on the whole nested product would couple blocks that the product keeps orthogonal, and `ProductManifold::new` refuses it with `Error::ProductFactor`.
The operator always receives the factor point and tangent vectors in the factor's own packing, so `ProductManifold::chart` keeps it unchanged.
The session steppers measure with the dot product of the packed vector or of the chart, and no fixed change of coordinates turns \(g(u, G_x v)\) into a dot product when \(G_x\) varies with \(x\).
A session therefore refuses a product with a tangent metric: a step fails with `Error::ProductTangentMetric`, `push_pair` returns `false` and `search_direction` fails.
`minimize_rtr`, `minimize_rtr_gauged` and `truncated_cg_riemannian` run in the metric.

# Gauge moves

A gauge move replaces the coordinates of the iterate by another representation of the same object, and leaves the objective's value unchanged.
The plane \(\{q : n \cdot (q - c) = d\}\) is named by its normal and its offset from a pivot \(c\), and the pivot can slide: moving it to \(c'\) and the offset to
\[
d' = d - n \cdot (c' - c)
\]
names the same plane.
The pivot is a parameter of the objective, not a coordinate of the manifold, so the move changes both the packed point and the function that reads it.

About a fixed pivot, turning the normal also moves the plane where it crosses the saddle region, so rotation and offset couple.
The two parametrizations differ by the shear \((n, d) \mapsto (n, d - n \cdot \Delta c)\), \(\Delta c = c' - c\): a turn \(u\) about \(c\) is, about \(c'\), the same turn with the offset changed by \(-u \cdot \Delta c\).
For the harmonic free energy at the optimal plane, the Hessian couples offset and rotation through \(\lambda_1 P q_0\), with \(q_0\) the saddle relative to the pivot and \(P\) the tangent projector of the normal, and adds \(|\lambda_1| P q_0 q_0^\top P\) to the rotation block.
Both vanish when the pivot is the in-plane minimum \(q^\ddagger + (r/s) H^+ n\) of the harmonic energy, the centre of the harmonic distribution on the plane, which at the optimum is the saddle.
Re-centring the pivot there after every step makes the Hessian at the optimum block-diagonal, with the harmonic metric as its rotation block.

/In the trust region./
`minimize_rtr_gauged` calls the gauge after every accepted step.
The step is accepted on the value before the move, since the ratio compares the model at \(x\) with the objective at the trial point, both in the old parametrization.
The value is evaluated again only when the gauge changed \(x\), because a gauge preserves it; the gradient always is, because a new parametrization changes it even when it leaves \(x\) as it was.
The next model, the stopping test and the returned `RtrMin` belong to the moved point, and the radius carries over.
A gauge that changes the value still runs, without the monotone decrease.
manopt's `options.hook` in `trustregions` does the same: it runs at the start of every iteration, before the stopping test, and when it moves \(x\) the solver evaluates the cost and gradient again.
It also runs after rejected steps, where an idempotent gauge has nothing to do.

/In a session./
`Solver::run_gauged` calls the gauge before every step but the first, so the returned report describes the point left in \(x\).
A session keeps the last point, value and gradient, and its next step builds a secant pair from them, reading any change of \(x\) between calls as a step.
Across a move that pair mixes two parametrizations: its change of gradient holds the shear, not curvature.
A gauge that changes \(x\) therefore rebases the session, as `Solver::rebase`.
The curvature memory (the L-BFGS pairs, the BFGS matrix, the trust radii) stays, the cached point goes, and the next step evaluates the objective afresh at the moved point.
The retained pairs come from nearby parametrizations, and the shear between them shrinks as the pivot converges.
On the plane test, re-centring before every step and running to a gradient norm of \(10^{-7}\), the three ways to treat a move took these numbers of steps:

| At a move                          | L-BFGS | Newton-CG | BFGS                      |
|------------------------------------+--------+-----------+---------------------------|
| keep the secant across it          |     50 |        34 | 111                       |
| forget all memory (`Solver::forget`) |   75 |       108 | not converged in 3000     |
| rebase (`Solver::rebase`)          |     33 |        34 | 111                       |

L-BFGS without the gauge takes 36 steps.
