# Sphere Hessians and the extension of the cost

The caller's \(\bar f\) is defined on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and many functions agree with it on the sphere.
`Sphere::ehess2rhess` keeps the Weingarten term explicit,
\[
\mathrm{Hess} f(x)[u] = (I - x x^\top) \nabla^2 \bar f(x)\, u - (x^\top \nabla \bar f(x))\, u,
\]
and every embedded kind that supplies `ehess2rhess` keeps its own term the same way.
The result does not depend on the extension.
If \(\bar f_1\) and \(\bar f_2\) agree on the sphere, then \(h ` \bar f_1 - \bar f_2\) vanishes there, so its gradient is normal: \(\nabla h(x) ` \mu(x)\, x\) with \(\mu = x^\top \nabla h\).
Differentiating along a curve on the sphere with velocity \(u\) gives \(\nabla^2 h(x)\, u ` (\mathrm{D} \mu(x)[u])\, x + \mu(x)\, u\), so \((I - x x^\top) \nabla^2 h(x)\, u ` \mu(x)\, u\), which the Weingarten term \(-(x^\top \nabla h(x))\, u = -\mu(x)\, u\) cancels.
Boumal's Corollary 5.47 states the general fact: the correction depends on the extension only through the normal part of its gradient.
On `SubspaceSphere` the gradient of \(h\) also has a part in \(U^\perp\), whose derivative stays in \(U^\perp\), and \(P_x\) removes both.

The degree-zero extension \(\bar f(x) ` f(x / \|x\|)\) is constant along rays, so \(x^\top \nabla \bar f ` 0\) on the sphere and the term vanishes: the projected Hessian alone is the Riemannian Hessian.
The session's dogleg step models the Hessian as \(Z^\top \nabla^2 \bar f\, Z\), with \(Z\) an orthonormal basis of the tangent space, and its Newton-CG and Newton-PCG steps as \(P \nabla^2 \bar f\, P + (I - P)\).
Neither has the Weingarten term, so both are exact for the degree-zero extension.
For another extension the model is off by \(x^\top \nabla \bar f\) times the identity on the tangent space, which at a minimizer is the Lagrange multiplier and does not vanish, and the steps converge linearly.
For \(\bar f(x) = x^\top A x\) the model is \(2A\) on the tangent space where the Hessian is \(2(A - \lambda_1 I)\), so near the lowest eigenvector each step keeps \(\lambda_1 / \lambda_j\) of the error along eigenvector \(j\), and the rate is \(\lambda_1 / \lambda_2\) when \(0 < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2\).
`tests/subspace_sphere.rs` measures that rate, \(1/2\) within 0.02, on a subspace sphere where \(\lambda_1 / \lambda_2 = 1/2\), against at most ten steps for the degree-zero extension \(x^\top A x / x^\top x\).
`minimize_rtr` uses `ehess2rhess` and converges quadratically with either.

# The optimal dividing plane

Section 4.6 of the optimal-hyperplane (OH-TST) design in `rgsaddle` lists what it needs from rgmin.
Its plane is a unit normal \(n\) on the sphere of the subspace the sampler moves in and a signed offset \(d\) from a pivot \(c\), so the manifold is \(S(U) \times \mathbb{R}\), and the drivers minimize \(f = -A\) for the free energy \(A\) of the plane.
`tests/plane_free_energy.rs` solves its harmonic model, \(A ` r^2 / (2s) + \tfrac{k_B T}{2} \ln(-s)\) with \(s ` n^\top H^+ n\) and \(r ` d - n \cdot (q^\ddagger - c)\), whose optimum is the unstable mode through the saddle \(q^\ddagger\), with \(f^* ` \tfrac{k_B T}{2} \ln |\lambda_1|\).
The items of section 4.6 map onto the crate as follows.
1. /A Euclidean factor./
   `ProductFactor::new(ManifoldKind::Euclidean, 1)` carries the offset.
   SPD(1) is the half-line \(d > 0\), and no metric on it lets the offset change sign.
   From a pivot at the origin the optimal offset of the test plane is \(e_1 \cdot q^\ddagger = -0.8\).
   On SPD(1) the retraction \(d + v + v^2 / (2d)\) never goes below \(d / 2\), and in the affine-invariant metric the gradient norm \(d\,|\partial f / \partial d|\) vanishes with \(d\), so the run stops on the gradient tolerance after 116 iterations at \(d \approx 5 \times 10^{-11}\) with \(f\) still 0.47 above \(f^*\).
2. /Weights and a preconditioner./
   `ProductFactor::with_weight` sets the block weights of the design's section 4.2, and `ProductFactor::with_metric` attaches a tangent metric, here the harmonic rotation block \(k_B T (I + |\lambda_1| H_\parallel^{-1})\) compressed to the tangent space.
   Both enter `egrad2rgrad` and every inner product of the trust region.
3. /A sphere of a subspace./
   `ManifoldKind::sphere_excluding` takes the centre-of-mass directions and fixed atoms, and `ManifoldKind::sphere_within` takes a rotation subspace.
4. /A gauge hook./
   `minimize_rtr_gauged` re-centres the pivot after each accepted step, and `Solver::run_gauged` does it between the steps of a session.
5. /Stochastic drivers./ Not here; see the limitations.
6. /A Hessian-vector oracle with an error bar and a harmonic preconditioner./ Not here; see the limitations.
7. /A convention for sphere Hessians./
   Both options of the design hold: `ehess2rhess` keeps the explicit Weingarten term for any extension, and the session steppers are exact for the degree-zero extension.

On the harmonic model with \(D ` 24\) coordinates, \(k_B T ` 0.3\), \(\lambda_1 = -1.5\) and in-plane curvatures from 0.05 to 8, `minimize_rtr` from a normal a few degrees off the unstable mode reaches the optimal plane in every metric, to \(10^{-10}\) in the gradient norm, the normal and \(f\):

| Metric on \((n, d)\)                                         | Outer iterations | Inner iterations |
|--------------------------------------------------------------+------------------+------------------|
| unit weights                                                 |                8 |               40 |
| block weight \(\ell^2 = 0.5\) on the normal                  |                7 |               35 |
| harmonic tangent metric, offset weight \(\vert\lambda_1\vert\) |              6 |               14 |
| the same, with the pivot re-centred after each step          |                6 |                8 |

Exact second derivatives keep the outer counts close; the metric shows in the inner solves.
At the optimum the harmonic metric makes the Hessian the identity plus the rank-two coupling of rotation and offset, and re-centring removes the coupling.
A session's L-BFGS in the block-weighted chart takes 36 steps, and 33 with `Solver::run_gauged` re-centring the pivot before each step.
The sampled loop of the design is `truncated_cg_riemannian` for the step and `RtrRadius::update` for a decrease measured outside the model; the test runs it with exact decreases in place of estimates.

# Comparison with manopt, Manifolds.jl, pymanopt and geomstats

At unit weights the product here is the product of:
- manopt `productmanifold` ([Boumal et al., JMLR 15, 1455 (2014)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/boumal14a.html)), source [a149c85](https://github.com/NicolasBoumal/manopt/blob/a149c85ca3cf23ca828d8bc6a6b125a4ac82d656/manopt/tools/productmanifold.m);
- ManifoldsBase.jl `ProductManifold`, used by Manifolds.jl and by the solvers of Manopt.jl ([Axen et al., ACM TOMS 49, 1 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3618296); [Bergmann, JOSS 7, 3866 (2022)](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.03866)), source [b16e9d6](https://github.com/JuliaManifolds/ManifoldsBase.jl/blob/b16e9d6f305a68385135092055cb8698d6c69e89/src/ProductManifold.jl);
- pymanopt `Product` ([Townsend et al., JMLR 17, 1 (2016)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v17/16-177.html)), source [35b022f](https://github.com/pymanopt/pymanopt/blob/35b022ff6043b893f32c903b428e811dea200dc2/src/pymanopt/manifolds/product.py);
- geomstats `ProductRiemannianMetric` ([Miolane et al., JMLR 21, 1 (2020)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v21/19-027.html)), source [5dd5cc2](https://github.com/geomstats/geomstats/blob/5dd5cc286a86f71ce9aed4f263539ec4bfa4c586/geomstats/geometry/product_manifold.py).
All five agree on the summed inner product and on the blockwise exponential and logarithm, and those that offer parallel transport carry it per factor.
manopt and pymanopt also convert Euclidean gradients and Hessians factor by factor, passing each factor its block of the full Euclidean Hessian action as here, so the cross terms of equation 5.12 arrive the same way.
ManifoldsBase.jl supplies the Weingarten map per factor for the same purpose, and geomstats has no such conversion.

| Aspect             | rgmin                         | manopt                | Manifolds.jl              | pymanopt     | geomstats                       |
|--------------------+-------------------------------+-----------------------+---------------------------+--------------+---------------------------------|
| weights            | \(w_i > 0\) per factor        | none                  | none                      | none         | per factor, `ScalarProductMetric` |
| points             | one packed vector             | struct of fields      | `ArrayPartition`          | list         | one vector, or stacked          |
| nested product     | flattened, weights multiply   | nested structs        | `×` flattens              | refused      | an ordinary factor              |
| missing operation  | `None` at the call            | field absent          | method error              | factor raises | numerical solver, else error    |
| distance           | weighted \(\ell_2\)           | \(\ell_2\)            | \(\ell_r\), default \(r = 2\) | \(\ell_2\) | \(\ell_2\)                      |
| typical distance   | weighted \(\ell_2\)           | \(\ell_2\)            | none                      | \(\ell_2\)   | none                            |
| random tangent     | none                          | scaled \(k^{-1/2}\)   | per factor                | scaled \(k^{-1/2}\) | per factor               |
| retraction choice  | one per kind                  | one per factory       | `ProductRetraction`       | one per factor | exponential                   |
| parallel transport | per factor, optional          | if all factors have it | per factor               | none         | per factor                      |
| injectivity radius | not exposed                   | not exposed           | minimum                   | not exposed  | minimum                         |
| power manifold     | unit-weight product           | `powermanifold`       | `PowerManifold`           | none         | `NFoldManifold`                 |
| subspace sphere    | kept or excluded basis        | two fixed subspaces   | symmetric matrices        | kept or excluded basis | none                  |
| preconditioner     | `TangentMetric`, in the metric | in truncated CG      | in truncated CG (Manopt.jl) | in truncated CG | none                       |
| point hook         | after accepted steps; sessions rebase | `options.hook` | step callbacks (Manopt.jl) | none       | none                            |

The differences in detail:
- /Weights./
  Only this product weighs its factors.
  manopt, Manifolds.jl and pymanopt build the element-wise sum of the factor metrics, and a caller who wants \(w_i g_i\) must write a scaled factor.
  geomstats removed the `scales` of `ProductManifold` and `ProductRiemannianMetric` in 2022 ([856c3ac](https://github.com/geomstats/geomstats/commit/856c3ac2104e)).
  It now scales a factor by equipping it with `ScalarProductMetric`, whose rules are the table of the metric section: inner products times \(s\); norms, distances and injectivity radius times \(\sqrt{s}\); sectional curvature times \(1/s\); exponential, logarithm and parallel transport unchanged.
  Its product reshape for such factors was fixed in November 2026 ([pull request 2203](https://github.com/geomstats/geomstats/pull/2203)).
  A weighted product here is a geomstats product of `ScalarProductMetric` factors.
- /Points./
  A point here is one `f64` vector holding each factor point in its kind's packing, column-major for `StiefelP` like manopt's `X(:)` and row-major for the symmetric kinds, so the session steppers and the C ABI see one array.
  manopt uses a struct with one named field per factor, Manifolds.jl a RecursiveArrayTools `ArrayPartition`, and pymanopt a list.
  geomstats concatenates the flattened factor points, or stacks them when every factor has the same shape.
- /Nesting./
  `ProductManifold::new` flattens a product factor into its blocks and multiplies the weights, so \((\mathcal{M}_1 \times \mathcal{M}_2) \times \mathcal{M}_3\) is a three-factor product.
  Manifolds.jl's `×` also flattens, without weights.
  manopt nests structs, pymanopt refuses a nested product, and geomstats treats it as an ordinary factor.
- /Optional operations./
  Here every `Manifold` method exists on every product.
  The exponential, logarithm, distance, parallel transport and `ehess2rhess` return `None` as soon as one factor lacks a closed form, and `minimize_rtr` then uses the Gauss-Newton Hessian.
  manopt defines a field such as `M.exp` or `M.ehess2rhess` only when all elements provide it, so a solver sees the absence before it starts.
  pymanopt always defines the method and the factor raises `NotImplementedError` at the call.
  Manifolds.jl fails with a method error, and geomstats falls back on a factor metric's numerical `exp_solver` and `log_solver` when it has them.
- /Gradient and Hessian conversion./
  manopt's and pymanopt's conversions have the blockwise structure of this one without the division by \(w_i\).
  manopt warns that a factor's `egrad2rgrad` or `ehess2rhess` written with `storedb` and `key` arguments will not receive them inside a product.
- /Distance and norm./
  Here the distance is the weighted root sum of squares, which is the Riemannian distance of \(g\).
  manopt, pymanopt and geomstats take the unweighted root sum of squares.
  Manifolds.jl's `distance(M, p, q, r)` and `norm(M, p, X, r)` take any \(\ell_r\) norm of the factor values, \(r = 2\) by default; for \(r \ne 2\) they are not the distance and norm of the product metric.
- /Typical distance and default radius./
  Here it is the weighted root sum of squares; manopt and pymanopt take the unweighted one, and both start their trust regions at \(\bar\Delta\) equal to it and \(\Delta_0 = \bar\Delta / 8\), pymanopt falling back on \(\sqrt{\dim \mathcal{M}}\).
  Manopt.jl's `trust_regions` defaults to \(\bar\Delta = \sqrt{\dim \mathcal{M}}\) ([01ae0f6](https://github.com/JuliaManifolds/Manopt.jl/blob/01ae0f62e90c9def032e8e32b3e4ffc988ca9288/src/solvers/trust_regions.jl)), and ManifoldsBase.jl and geomstats have no typical distance.
- /Random tangent vectors./
  manopt and pymanopt scale each factor's random unit tangent vector by \(k^{-1/2}\), so the tuple has unit length in the unweighted metric.
  There is no random point or tangent here.
- /Retraction and transport choice./
  Here each kind has one retraction and one transport.
  manopt uses each factory's `retr` and `transp`, with `retr2`, `isotransp` and `paralleltransp` when all elements provide them.
  Manifolds.jl composes `ProductRetraction`, `InverseProductRetraction` and `ProductVectorTransport` from any per-factor methods.
  pymanopt uses each factor's `retraction` and `transport`, and geomstats works with the exponential and logarithm.
- /Parallel transport and isometry./
  Here parallel transport is per factor, `None` when a factor has none, and `transport_is_isometric` is the conjunction over the factors.
  manopt offers `paralleltransp` and `isotransp` when every element does, Manifolds.jl and geomstats transport per factor, and pymanopt has no parallel transport.
- /Injectivity radius and curvature./
  Neither is exposed here.
  Manifolds.jl takes the minimum injectivity radius of the factors, computes the sectional curvature of a product exactly, bounds it by the factor bounds and 0 when \(k \ge 2\), and calls a product flat when every factor is.
  geomstats takes the minimum injectivity radius, and `ScalarProductMetric` scales it by \(\sqrt{s}\).
  `ProductManifold::is_flat` here means that every factor keeps a straight step on its set, a different notion from the zero curvature of Manifolds.jl's `is_flat`.
- /Power manifold./
  `ProductManifold::power` and `ManifoldKind::power` are unit-weight products, and Oblique stays a dedicated kind with its own column loops.
  manopt's `powermanifold`, Manifolds.jl's `PowerManifold` and geomstats' `NFoldManifold` are separate types, and pymanopt has none.
- /Metric matrix and signature./
  geomstats' `ProductRiemannianMetric` also offers a block-diagonal `metric_matrix` and the summed signature.
  The trait here has only `inner` on tangent vectors.
- /Subspace spheres./
  pymanopt's `SphereSubspaceIntersection` and `SphereSubspaceComplementIntersection` ([sphere.py at 35b022f](https://github.com/pymanopt/pymanopt/blob/35b022ff6043b893f32c903b428e811dea200dc2/src/pymanopt/manifolds/sphere.py)) are the counterparts of `within` and `excluding`, with the same projector, Weingarten term, exponential, logarithm and distance.
  They build the dense projector \(Q Q^\top\) from a QR factorization of the spanning columns and do not refuse a rank-deficient matrix, and their retraction normalizes \(x + v\) without projecting back onto the subspace, so rounding off it is not removed.
  manopt and Manifolds.jl have the spheres of fixed subspaces only: unit-norm symmetric matrices (manopt's `spheresymmetricfactory`, Manifolds.jl's `SphereSymmetricMatrices`) and, in manopt, the unit tangent vectors at one point of a manifold (`tangentspherefactory`).
  geomstats has none.
- /Preconditioners./
  manopt's `problem.precon` ([trs_tCG.m](https://github.com/NicolasBoumal/manopt/blob/a149c85ca3cf23ca828d8bc6a6b125a4ac82d656/manopt/solvers/trustregions/trs_tCG.m)), pymanopt's `Problem(preconditioner=...)` and the `preconditioner` keyword of Manopt.jl's `trust_regions` approximate the inverse Hessian inside the truncated CG of the trust region.
  A `TangentMetric` gives the same iterates, but it is part of the manifold: `egrad2rgrad` returns the preconditioned gradient, so a first-order or sampled driver sees it as well, and the inner and outer stopping tests read lengths in it.
  geomstats has no trust region.
- /Point hooks./
  manopt's `options.hook` (`applyHook`) replaces the iterate at the start of every iteration of `trustregions` and `steepestdescent`, before the stopping test, and the solver evaluates the cost and gradient again when it moved; the other solvers do not call it.
  `minimize_rtr_gauged` has the same semantics after accepted steps, and `Solver::run_gauged` adds the rebase that a solver with curvature memory needs.
  Manopt.jl's solver states take callbacks before and after each step (`:BeforeStep`, `:Step`), which receive the state and may change it ([callback.jl at 01ae0f6](https://github.com/JuliaManifolds/Manopt.jl/blob/01ae0f62e90c9def032e8e32b3e4ffc988ca9288/src/base/state/callback.jl)).
  pymanopt and geomstats have no hook.

# Reconciliation with the earlier manifold branches

Two earlier branches carried product designs, and the product kind of this page supersedes both.

`feat/manifold-api-060` added `RiemannianManifold` in `cdc8f5dd`, a product of Stiefel and SPD factors over caller-owned column-major slices.
The OH-TST design pins rgmin at `d3f94d11`, a commit that already has it, and the product kind was built on top of it.
It has QR and polar Stiefel retractions, the Edelman, Arias and Smith exponential, SPD under the affine-invariant and log-Euclidean metrics, and a `gradient_step` helper.
It sits beside `ManifoldKind`, so no session can step it.
It implemented the old `Manifold` trait, whose only metric was the dot product, so a driver would have measured its affine-invariant SPD gradient \(X \nabla f X\) in another metric; its trait implementation now forwards `inner` to the factor metrics.
Here the product is a `ManifoldKind` over every kind, with weights, and the trait carries `inner`, so gradient and metric agree.
Stiefel frames keep the column-major packing that both designs use.
`RiemannianManifold` stays, and its polar retraction and log-Euclidean metric have no `ManifoldKind`.
The `Spd` kind already took the affine-invariant gradient \(X \nabla f X\), and it now carries the matching inner product \(\mathrm{tr}(X^{-1} U X^{-1} V)\) and Hessian, so it enters a product in that metric.
Sessions still form their secant pairs in the dot product of the packed coordinates, as before, while `minimize_rtr` measures `Spd` in its own metric.

The rest of the branch, up to `7ea30e08`, binds `RiemannianManifold` outside Rust.
Its C handles are built by `rgmin_manifold_stiefel`, `rgmin_manifold_spd` and `rgmin_manifold_product`, released by `rgmin_manifold_free`, and passed to one function per slice method, `gradient_step` included.
C++ wraps them in `rgmin::Manifold`, and the Python module `rgmin.manifold` has `Stiefel`, `SPD` and `Product` classes over NumPy arrays, a product point being a tuple of factor arrays.
No function hands a handle to a session, whose manifold stays the unrelated `rgmin_manifold_t` token.
The three bindings stay as they were and reach no `ManifoldKind` product.
The handles hold ABI minor 41 and the line's minors 42 and 43 follow, so `rgmin_solver_set_power` takes minor 44.

A caller of `RiemannianManifold` who wants a session or the trust region moves over as follows:

| `RiemannianManifold`                 | `ManifoldKind`                                                               |
|--------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `stiefel(n, 1, _)`                   | `ManifoldKind::Sphere`, or `sphere_within` and `sphere_excluding` for a subspace |
| `stiefel(n, p, _)`                   | `ManifoldKind::stiefel(n, p)`, with the QR retraction                         |
| `spd(p, _)`                          | `ManifoldKind::Spd` at packed length \(p^2\), in the affine-invariant metric  |
| no flat factor                       | `ManifoldKind::Euclidean`                                                    |
| `product(parts)`                     | `ManifoldKind::product` of `ProductFactor` values, with weights and tangent metrics |
| slice methods writing into `out`     | `Manifold` methods on `Array1` that return the result                        |
| `gradient_step`                      | a session step, or `minimize_rtr`                                            |
| C handles, C++ `rgmin::Manifold`     | kept; `rgmin_solver_set_power` selects a power in a session                  |
| Python `rgmin.manifold`              | kept, over the slice methods                                                 |

The plane of the design, `product([stiefel(D, 1, _), spd(1, _)])` with `RiemannianManifold`, becomes
`ManifoldKind::product([ProductFactor::new(ManifoldKind::sphere_excluding(e)?, D).with_weight(l2), ProductFactor::new(ManifoldKind::Euclidean, 1)])`
with `e` the excluded directions and `l2` the block weight \(\ell^2\), or `with_metric` in place of `with_weight` for a harmonic metric on the normal.

`feat/power-manifold` (`3bb6f1df`) added `ManifoldKind::Power` over four factors (Euclidean, sphere, MwRigid, rigid quotient), `Solver::set_power`, a C setter with private factor codes 0 to 3 and the token `RGMIN_MANIFOLD_POWER`, and `minimize_rtr` in the dot-product metric.
The power is now a special case of the product.
`ManifoldKind::power` builds a unit-weight `ProductManifold` of any kind, so a power inherits the metric, exponential, logarithm, Hessian and chart instead of repeating them.
`Solver::set_power` keeps its signature, its rule for `MwRigid` masses (one molecule reused on every copy, or every copy's masses in order) and its per-block Eckart projection.
`rgmin_solver_set_power` keeps its signature but reads the factor as an `rgmin_manifold_t` token for any kind without shape parameters, in place of the private codes.
The branch never shipped, so no ABI user sees the change.
`RGMIN_MANIFOLD_POWER` is not added: a token cannot carry the factor, block and count, and the branch's default, two Euclidean blocks of length one, is just \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
`minimize_rtr` is ported and now runs in `inner` with `ehess2rhess` and the typical distance.
Oblique stays its own kind, the power of spheres with column loops of its own.

# How the derivation is checked

`tests/product_manifold.rs` checks each section numerically on a quartic \(\bar f(x) = \tfrac12 x^\top A x + b^\top x + \tfrac14 \sum_i x_i^4\) whose dense \(A\) couples every block:
- manopt's `checkgradient` and `checkhessian`: the remainders of the first- and second-order models along \(t \mapsto R_x(t v)\) and \(t \mapsto \exp_x(t v)\) have slopes 2 and 3 in \(\log t\) (Boumal, sections 4.8 and 6.8), on the weighted \(\mathbb{R}^4 \times S^3\) along both curves, on \(S^2 \times SO(3)\) with the Hessian along the exponential, and on every kind with a closed-form geodesic times a weighted \(\mathbb{R}^2\);
- \(g(\mathrm{grad} f, v) = \nabla \bar f^\top v\), tangency of the gradient and of the Hessian action, and symmetry of the Hessian in \(g\);
- the retraction and the exponential stay on the manifold for steps from \(10^{-3}\) to \(10\);
- transport lands in the target tangent space, parallel transport preserves \(g\), and a product of flat factors with weights 2, 1/4 and 1 transports isometrically;
- the locking condition with \(\beta ` 1\): the velocity of \(t \mapsto \exp_x(t d)\) at \(t ` 1\), by central differences, equals `parallel_transport_along(x, d, d)`;
- \(\log_x(\exp_x(v)) ` v\), \(\mathrm{dist}(x, \exp_x(v)) ` \|v\|\) and the weighted typical distance;
- L-BFGS, steepest descent, the session Newton-CG trust region and `minimize_rtr` reach the minimum of a coupled Rayleigh quotient and quadratic on the hyperplane, \(\tfrac12 (p - c)^\top B (p - c) + n^\top A n + \kappa ((p - c)^\top n)^2\), whose value is the lowest eigenvalue of \(A\);
- the unit test of the chart section, and the rigid factors keep their mass-weighted centres.

`tests/subspace_sphere.rs` checks the sphere of a subspace:
- the `checkgradient` and `checkhessian` slopes along the retraction and the exponential;
- a kept basis and its excluded complement give the same projector, nearest point, tangent projection and retraction;
- retraction and exponential steps stay on the sphere and in the subspace, the logarithm inverts the exponential at the right distance, and both transports land in the arrival tangent space;
- the Hessian is the same for \(\bar f\) and for \(\bar f + (\|x\|^2 - 1)(c^\top x + 2)\), and equals the projected Hessian of the degree-zero extension by central differences, on `SubspaceSphere` and on `Sphere`;
- L-BFGS and `minimize_rtr` find the lowest mode inside the subspace of a Rayleigh quotient whose two lowest modes are excluded, which the whole sphere reaches instead;
- the session Newton-CG rates of the section on sphere Hessians.

`tests/plane_free_energy.rs` solves the harmonic plane of the section on the optimal dividing plane and asserts the comparisons made there.
It also checks that the gradient is the Riesz vector of the harmonic metric, runs the sampled trust-region loop, the gauged trust region and the gauged session, and checks that sessions refuse a tangent metric.

# Limitations

- The session's dogleg, Newton-CG and Newton-PCG steps model the Hessian of a curved factor without its Weingarten term, which is exact for the degree-zero extension only (see the section on sphere Hessians).
  On the hyperplane test, with \(n^\top A n\) on the normal, the Newton-CG trust region converges at the rate \(\lambda_1 / \lambda_2 = 1/2\) of the two lowest eigenvalues of \(A\).
  `minimize_rtr` uses `ehess2rhess` and converges quadratically on the same problem: its gradient norm goes from \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) to \(2 \times 10^{-9}\) to \(10^{-16}\) in its last three iterations.
- A tangent metric costs its product the exponential, logarithm, distance, parallel transport and isometric transport, `typical_dist` ignores it, and its Hessian is the model \(G^{-1} \mathrm{Hess}\), exact at critical points only.
  Sessions refuse it with `Error::ProductTangentMetric`.
- The stochastic drivers of the OH-TST design (its item 5) are not here: stochastic gradient ascent with a step schedule and iterate averaging, the norm test on the sample size, a trust region that weighs a measured decrease against its standard error, and `NoiseFloor` driven by a caller's covariance.
  Each needs an interface for noisy values and gradients with their covariance, which the `Manifold` trait and the sessions do not have, and convergence tests on sampled objectives.
  `Control::noise_floor` stops a session at \(c \sqrt{n_\mathrm{free}}\, \varepsilon_g\) for a caller's gradient noise \(\varepsilon_g\), a scalar in place of a covariance, and `minimize_rtr` has no such stop.
  The deterministic core of such a driver is here: `egrad2rgrad` gives the preconditioned direction, `truncated_cg_riemannian` the trust-region step in the metric and `RtrRadius::update` the radius from a decrease measured outside the model.
- Item 6, a Hessian-vector product with an error bar and a preconditioner built from the harmonic model, is not here either.
  The truncated CG treats every Hessian-vector product as exact, and its curvature and boundary tests would need a confidence level to take an estimate.
  A low-rank-plus-scalar model can already be supplied as a `TangentMetric`, or as an `hvp::Preconditioner` for the Euclidean `hvp::steihaug_pcg`.
- The QR retraction of SO(3) is first order, so the numerical Hessian check on \(S^2 \times SO(3)\) runs along the exponential.
- `Multinomial` projects Fisher-orthogonally but keeps the dot product as its inner product, so its gradient does not represent the differential in that inner product, and the derivative tests leave it out.
  The doubly stochastic kinds carry the Fisher inner product and are consistent.
- `Spd` carries the affine-invariant metric, in which its gradient, inner product and Hessian agree and its retraction \(x + v + \tfrac12 v x^{-1} v\) is second order.
  Its transport, the identity on tangents, is not an isometry of that metric.
- `Multinomial` and its doubly stochastic variants, `MwRigid` and `RigidQuotient` have no Hessian or geodesic closed forms, and `StiefelP` and `Spd` have a Hessian but no exponential, logarithm or parallel transport.
  A product containing one returns `None` for those operations; projection, retraction, transport and the gradient still work.
- A weighted product refuses the settings that read raw coordinates, with `Error::ProductChart`.
- The C ABI selects powers only, through `rgmin_solver_set_power`.
  A general weighted product has to carry its parameterized factors (the sizes of Oblique, Stiefel and the complex kinds), their weights and the basis of a subspace sphere across the ABI.
  A descriptor struct or composed handles like those of `RiemannianManifold` can do that, and either is a separate ABI design.
  Tangent metrics and gauges are Rust callbacks: the C ABI exposes sessions, which refuse tangent metrics, and has no entry for `minimize_rtr`, so both wait for a callback design.
  The Python module `rgmin.manifold` binds the slice methods of `RiemannianManifold` and no `ManifoldKind`, so a Python product waits for a binding of `ManifoldKind`.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/python-threads.org`

# What you can share

A `SolverConfig` does not change after it is built. Any number of
threads can read one config and build their own solvers from it.

A `Solver` is used by one thread at a time. If a second thread calls
`step` or `step_hess` while the first call is still running, that
second call raises `RuntimeError` and says the solver is in use. Two
different solvers can run at the same time, including when the
interpreter is free-threaded and `sys._is_gil_enabled()` is false.

The array you pass to `step` is updated in place. The objective
receives its own copy of the coordinates, so keeping that array after
`step` returns is safe. Do not let two threads call the same objective
if the objective mutates a shared object.

# Calculators

ASE calculators are not thread-safe. Each thread needs its own
calculator. Sharing one calculator across threads is not supported.

rgmin guarantees three things. A `SolverConfig` can be shared. A
`Solver` is entered by one thread, and a second call raises
`RuntimeError`. The objective is handed its own copy of the
coordinates.

The optimizer keeps a lock around calls on one calculator unless that
calculator sets `reentrant` to true. The lock only stops those calls
from overlapping. It does not make the calculator safe to share.
`import rgmin` does not import ASE. The ASE classes live in `rgmin.ase`.

# Results

The trajectory of one solver does not depend on how many Python
threads or how many Rayon threads are running other solvers. The
default build does not turn on the Rust parallel feature, so extra
threads do not speed up a single solve.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/quasi-newton.org`

Newton's method prices a step at one Hessian solve; the secant family
refuses to pay it. This page derives what the crate's quasi-Newton
solvers (`src/qn.rs`, `src/lbfgs.rs`) actually compute, and why the
warm-restart and recognition hooks on the session are correctness-
preserving.

# The secant condition

After a step `s = x_new - x_old` with gradient change
`y = g_new - g_old`, any model Hessian `B` worth keeping should
reproduce the observed curvature: B s = y. In inverse form, with
H ` B^-1, the condition reads H y ` s. One equation cannot determine a
matrix, so each method adds a minimality principle. BFGS chooses the
inverse update closest to the old `H` in a weighted Frobenius norm
subject to the secant condition and symmetry, which lands on

  H_new = (I - rho s y^T) H (I - rho y s^T) + rho s s^T,
  rho   = 1 / (y . s).

The update preserves positive definiteness exactly when the curvature
pair condition y . s > 0 holds, which the strong Wolfe curvature
condition guarantees at an accepted line-search point. The default
step does not search the line. It is the eOn cap: the first step
probes curvature, and a proposal at least as long as the cap clears
the memory. `LbfgsStep::Wolfe` is the opt-in search that enforces the
condition before the step is accepted. `LbfgsStep::Scaled` shortens
the two-loop step and keeps the pair.

# The two-loop recursion

Storing `H` costs n^2; limited-memory BFGS stores the last `m` pairs
(s_i, y_i) and applies the update implicitly. Unrolling the BFGS
formula `m` times around a seed matrix H0 gives the two-loop
recursion (Nocedal and Wright 7.4):

  q = g
  for i ` m-1 .. 0:   alpha_i ` rho_i (s_i . q);  q = q - alpha_i y_i
  r = H0 q
  for i ` 0 .. m-1:   beta ` rho_i (y_i . r);     r = r + (alpha_i - beta) s_i
  direction = -r

with the standard scalar seed H0 = (s . y) / (y . y) I from the most
recent pair, a one-parameter fit of the average curvature along the
last step; positivity of that scalar is again the pair condition.
An installed exponential preconditioner replaces that scalar.
The middle product of the two-loop solves with the preconditioner,
so the initial inverse Hessian is taken from it: `H0 = P^{-1}`.
Packwood, Kermode, Mones, Bernstein, Woolley, Gould, Ortner, and
Csányi, /A universal preconditioner for simulating condensed phase
materials/, J. Chem. Phys. 144, 164109 (2016)
([10.1063/1.4947024](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4947024);
@@rst::cite:`packwoodUniversalPreconditionerSimulating2016`@@).
A dense pair or Lindh matrix passed into the two-loop still wins.
With no preconditioner the scalar seed above is unchanged.
Every dot and axpy in the crate's two-loop routes through the
`vecops` seam, so the recursion is written once and the storage
backend (serial, `par`, and by design a later device backend) is a
detail behind four functions.

# The geometry step

This step runs when the caller has opted into `LbfgsStep::Wolfe` and
also set a per-atom cap (`set_atom_maxmove`). It ignores `set_accept`.
The default session step is the line-search-free cap, not this
geometry step. A HiGHS feasible set and a non-Euclidean manifold
stay on their own paths.

The initial scale is selected from the size of the nominal steepest
trial. A trial that exceeds the per-atom cap by at least 64 times
receives one directional-curvature probe; ordinary trials start from
`H0 = 0.1 I` without spending that force call. The probe is
`x + 0.01 u`, with `u` the unit force, clipped to the objective
bounds before it is evaluated. The quotient divides by the
displacement that remains along `u`. A probe the box reduces to
nothing, or a non-positive result, clears the memory and the step
is steepest descent scaled to the cap. Later iterations set
`H0 = (s . y) / (y . y)` when both dots are positive. Negative
curvature clears the stored pairs and uses that same steepest step.
The stiffness probe uses monotone energy acceptance. An ordinary
start admits an energy below the largest of the last five accepted
values.

An installed exponential preconditioner replaces that scalar seed.
The two-loop applies `P^{-1}` in its place, and a reset that would
have stepped along `h0` times the force steps along `P^{-1}` times
the force. The negative-curvature step and the short fallback after
ten halvings keep the coefficients 1000 and one tenth, applied to
`P^{-1}` times the force. A failed solve with `P` falls back to the
scalar seed. The per-atom cap still limits the displacement.

An uncapped direction longer than the cap, or one that opposes the
force, also clears the memory and replaces the direction with that
capped seed. The trial is kept when the energy rises by at most
1e-8. The step is halved at most ten times. If none of those trials
pass, the memory is cleared and a short steepest step, one tenth of
the preconditioned force and then the cap, is taken.

# The capped step

`LbfgsStep::Capped` is the default. `LbfgsStep::Wolfe` opts into
the line search. `set_atom_maxmove` replaces the cap while the
step is capped. The geometry step above runs when the caller has
opted into `Wolfe` and also set a per-atom cap.

The direction is the same two-loop. The initial inverse Hessian is
the Nocedal-Wright scale `(s · y) / (y · y)` on the latest stored
pair (equation 7.20)
@@rst::cite:`nocedalNumericalOptimization2006`@@.
An installed exponential preconditioner still replaces that scalar.
The step is then shortened so the longest per-atom displacement is
at most the caller's cap. The cap is the only length in the rule.
An empty memory has no curvature yet, so the step follows the force
and has that length. A direction that is not a descent direction
clears the memory and does the same. A pair with `s · y` below the
usual relative-curvature gate is not stored. A pair that passes the
gate is kept when the step was shortened: the cap changes the
length, and the stored pairs still describe the curvature.

One evaluation is taken at the trial. A non-finite quasi-Newton
trial is retried once along the force. A second non-finite trial
leaves the point and the pairs as they were. `Lbfgs::ftol`, when
positive, still ends the relaxation after a step that decreases
the value by little.

# Stale pairs and the cautious update

A pair with y . s <= 0 would corrupt the inverse model, so the update
skips it; the `cautious` knob (Li-Fukushima) additionally requires
y . s >= eps norm(s)^alpha before a pair enters the history, which
keeps far-from-quadratic steps from polluting the memory. Skipping is
always sound: the two-loop over any subset of valid pairs is the BFGS
inverse built from exactly those pairs.

# Bounds: the generalized Cauchy point

`Lbfgs::minimize_box` keeps the same pairs and replaces the two-loop direction with the step of limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno with bounds (L-BFGS-B).
Byrd, Lu, Nocedal and Zhu, /A limited memory algorithm for bound constrained optimization/, Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM) Journal on Scientific Computing 16, 1190 (1995) ([10.1137/0916069](https://doi.org/10.1137/0916069); @@rst::cite:`byrdLimitedMemoryAlgorithm1995`@@).
The step needs `B` rather than `H`, so it uses the compact form of Byrd, Nocedal and Schnabel, Mathematical Programming 63, 129 (1994) ([10.1007/BF01582063](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01582063); @@rst::cite:`byrdRepresentationsQuasinewtonMatrices1994`@@):

#+begin_example
B ` theta I - W M W^T,   W ` [Y, theta S],
M^-1 = [[-D, L^T], [L, theta S^T S]],
#+end_example

with theta = (y^T y) / (s^T y) from the newest pair, `D` the diagonal of `s_i^T y_i`, and `L` the strictly lower triangle of S^T Y.
Both forms describe the same matrix when the two-loop recursion seeds with 1/theta.

The bounded step built on this matrix has two parts.
The generalized Cauchy point is the first local minimizer of the quadratic model along the projected steepest-descent path clip(x - t g, lo, hi).
That path is piecewise linear and bends where a coordinate meets its bound.
The search visits the bends in order of t and updates the slope and curvature of the model in O(m^2) work per bend (algorithm CP of the paper).
The coordinates that the Cauchy point leaves on a bound stay there.
One reduced Newton step moves the other coordinates.
It costs a 2m by 2m solve (section 5.1).
If that point leaves the box, it is projected back.
The projection is kept when it is still a descent direction; otherwise the step is cut back to the box.
That test is the remark of Morales and Nocedal, Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Transactions on Mathematical Software 38, 1 (2011) ([10.1145/2049662.2049669](https://doi.org/10.1145/2049662.2049669); @@rst::cite:`moralesRemarkAlgorithm7782011`@@).
The strong Wolfe search runs along the segment from x to that point and never steps outside the box.
The Fortran 77 code of Zhu, Byrd, Lu and Nocedal, ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software 23, 550 (1997) ([10.1145/279232.279236](https://doi.org/10.1145/279232.279236); @@rst::cite:`zhuAlgorithm778Lbfgsb1997`@@), as translated to C in SciPy 1.18.1 (commit e4e854ea, `scipy/optimize/src/lbfgsb.c`, routines `cauchy` and `subsm`), is the reference for the details.

With no finite bound the Cauchy point meets no bend and the reduced step covers every coordinate.
The end point is then x - H g, the two-loop direction up to rounding, and the unit test `unbounded_direction_is_the_two_loop_direction` checks that to 1e-12.
`Lbfgs::minimize` stays on its own step rule. The default is the eOn cap.
`LbfgsStep::Wolfe` opts into the search `minimize_box` uses.

# Session hooks: forget, watched, recognized

`Solver` (and anneal's `WarmLbfgs` face over it) exposes three
lifecycle hooks whose safety arguments are one sentence each:

- `forget()` clears the pair history. The next step is plain steepest
  descent scaled by the seed; every stored invariant is vacuous.
- `minimize_watched` runs a caller predicate per accepted iterate and
  stops early when asked. Stopping early returns an accepted iterate,
  so every property of the trajectory up to that point stands.
- `minimize_recognized` additionally lets the caller substitute a
  known result (energy and coordinates) when it recognizes the basin
  mid-descent, returning a flag that says the substitution happened.
  The optimizer never manufactures the substitute; it only carries the
  caller's answer out, so the correctness burden sits exactly where
  the knowledge is. The identity and refund tests in
  `tests/lbfgs_state.rs` pin both behaviors.

# Non-finite input is not convergence

A gradient with a NaN component has no norm worth trusting; the crate
maps any non-finite gradient to an infinite norm in both the Euclidean
and infinity norms (`vecops::nrminf` documents the rule as: a broken
vector is never a small one). The test
`a_nan_gradient_is_not_convergence` holds the L-BFGS driver to it, and
the C ABI returns NaN-filled gradients on callback failure for the
same reason: a consumer must never read half-written storage as a
small residual.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/quickmin.org`

Quick-min keeps a velocity and damps it by a projection before an
explicit Euler step. Write `F = -∇f` and `Δt` for the time step. The
reference update is

: v ← (v · F / |F|²) F    when v · F ≥ 0 and |F| > 0
: v ← 0                   otherwise
: v ← v + Δt F
: Δx = Δt v

`quickmin_baseline` is that update and nothing else. A negative
projection takes the second branch, so the velocity that enters the
Euler kick has no component opposing `F`. A zero force has no
direction and takes the same branch.

The session adds three pieces that the other first-order methods
already own.

The displacement cap is `Solver::set_atom_maxmove` or
`Control::maxmove`. When it shortens `Δx`, the velocity is multiplied
by `|Δx taken| / |Δx proposed|`. That is the ratio FIRE uses after its
own cap. The next projection then sees the motion that happened. On

: E = ½ (y - 0.2 x)² + 0.02 x²

from `(2, 0)` with `Δt = 0.2` and cap `0.08`, eighty reference steps
that keep the uncapped velocity stay above `10⁻⁷`, and the same steps
with the rescale fall below `10⁻⁸`.

The time step uses FIRE's factors: `n_min = 5`, `f_inc = 1.1`,
`f_dec = 0.5`, `Δt_max = 2.5 Δt₀`. More than `n_min` steps with
`F · v > 0` grow `Δt`. `F · v < 0` shrinks it, down to `10⁻¹²`; the
velocity on that branch is already zero from the reference rule.
`F · v = 0` leaves `Δt` alone. A resting velocity is not an uphill
step, and halving the caller's `Δt` before any motion only slows the
opening. On `E = ½ x²` from `x = 1` with `Δt₀ = 0.05`, the growing
step reaches `|x| < 10⁻³` in fewer iterations than the fixed step.
`Solver::set_quickmin_adapt(false)` selects the fixed reference step.

A cell block is an index `at`. Coordinates `[0, at)` and `[at, n)`
each take the reference replacement on their own force, then the Euler
kick uses the shared `Δt`. A cell velocity that opposes the stress is
zeroed even when the atomic alignment keeps `v · F` positive for the
whole vector. One joint projection would replace both blocks by a
single component along the joint force and spend atomic momentum on
the opposing cell direction. On `E = ½ (x² + c²)` at `(-1, 1)` with
`v = (3, 1)`, `F = (1, -1)` and `Δt = 0.1`, the split step reaches a
lower value than the joint projection, and the cell velocity after the
replacement is only the Euler kick `Δt F_c`.
`Solver::set_quickmin_cell` sets the index. The C entry is
`RGMIN_QUICKMIN` and `rgmin_solver_set_quickmin_cell` (ABI minor 29).

# Options and what the benchmark keeps

`Solver::set_quickmin_options` takes `QuickMinOptions`. `rgmin()` is
the session above. `eon()` is eOn's `Quickmin::step`: fixed `Δt`, one
projection, and a capped step that leaves the velocity at its
uncapped value. `per_atom()` projects each xyz triple of the atomic
block on its own force, so one atom moving against its force stops
without stopping the others. `curvature_cap = Some(c)` bounds `Δt` by
`c / sqrt(λ̂)`, with `λ̂ = |y| / |s|` from the last step's force
difference.

On `E = λ x² / 2` with the projection inactive, the step is the
symplectic Euler map with characteristic polynomial
`r² - (2 - h) r + 1`, `h = Δt² λ`. Its roots stay on the unit circle for
`0 ≤ h ≤ 4`, so `Δt < 2 / sqrt(λ_max)` is the stability limit. A step
from rest moves `Δt² F` and lowers the energy exactly when `h < 2`;
with `λ̂` equal to the mode's curvature, `c < sqrt(2)` keeps that.
With a kept velocity `v = c F` the step length along `F` is
`Δt (c + Δt)`, and `c` grows while the walker stays on one side, so
the eOn step can raise the energy even under `Δt² λ_max < 2`
(`validation/quickmin.py`). The projection itself never lengthens
`v` and leaves no component along `-F`
(`formal/RgminContracts/QuickMin.lean`); in binary64 it can lengthen
`v` by at most `B(n) - 1` relative, 7 machine epsilons for `n = 6`
(`validation/quickmin.sollya`).

`bench/atomistic` (rgpot potentials, 5 starts each, per-atom cap 0.2,
`fmax < 0.01`), mean force calls and converged starts:

| options                    | LJ38          | Pt7 island | Al slab |
|----------------------------+---------------+------------+---------|
| `eon()`                    | 2001 (0 of 5) |       18.6 |    24.6 |
| `rgmin()`                  | 1344 (4 of 5) |       19.6 |    27.6 |
| `per_atom()`               | 645 (5 of 5)  |       32.0 |    28.2 |
| `rgmin()`, `cap Some(0.7)` | 1167 (5 of 5) |       20.0 |    27.6 |
| FIRE                       | 411           |       50.6 |    60.2 |
| FIRE 2.0 (Guénolé 2020)    | 871           |       26.0 |    33.8 |
| L-BFGS                     | 169           |       10.0 |    14.0 |

The eOn options never converge LJ38 from random packings in 2000
steps; the FIRE time step is what converges it. The per-atom
projection halves the LJ38 calls and costs 12 calls on the seven-atom
island, so it is an option, not the default. A restart or a backtrack
after an energy rise, a ten-fold `Δt_max`, and dropping the clamp
rescale moved the LJ38 mean by at most 9 calls and the others by at
most 0.4, and none of them converged another start; they were removed.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/randomized.org`

The crate's one use of randomized numerical linear algebra is the
Nystrom preconditioner for the matrix-free Newton path. The design
rule it obeys is worth stating before the math: randomness may change
how fast an answer arrives, never which answer arrives. CG under any
symmetric positive definite preconditioner converges to the same
step; the preconditioner is a unit system for the iteration, not an
opinion about the solution. This page derives the sketch and pins
where each half of that claim is proved.

# Why a preconditioner pays here

CG's iteration count grows with the spread of the Hessian's spectrum.
Cluster and kernel Hessians typically carry a few stiff modes over a
soft bulk -- bond-stretch scales over collective, floppy ones. A
preconditioner that captures the stiff subspace and rescales it down
to the bulk flattens the effective spectrum, and the iteration count
drops to that of the easy part. The stiff subspace is low-rank, which
is exactly what a randomized sketch finds cheaply.

# The sketch (Frangella, Tropp, Udell)

Draw a random test block Omega (n x k; the crate uses Rademacher
entries, +-1, drawn from a seeded generator so a rebuild at the same
point is reproducible) and pay `k` Hessian actions for Y = H Omega.
With the stabilizing shift nu, the Nystrom approximation is

  H_nys ` Y_nu (Omega^T Y_nu)^-1 Y_nu^T,   Y_nu ` Y + nu Omega,

a rank-k surrogate that agrees with `H` on the sketched subspace.
Factoring the small k x k core by a Jacobi eigensolve and thin-
factoring through the Gram matrix B^T B yields H_nys = U L U^T with
orthonormal `U` and eigenvalue estimates `L`. The preconditioner then
equalizes the captured modes down to the smallest kept eigenvalue mu:

  P^-1 r = r + U ( diag(mu / (l_i + mu)) - I ) U^T r,

which damps each captured stiff mode by mu / (l_i + mu) and passes the
orthogonal complement through untouched.

Two Lean facts in
[Spectral.lean](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/blob/develop/proofs/lean/Rgmin/Spectral.lean) pin the
construction's legitimacy:

- `sumSq_nonneg` (with `sq_nonneg`): a Gram quadratic form is a sum of
  squares, so B B^T cannot manufacture negative curvature; the sketch
  is positive semidefinite by construction, not by luck.
- `shifted_weight_pos` / `equalized_weight_bounds`: with nonnegative
  kept eigenvalues and a positive shift, every weight the solve divides
  by is positive and every damping factor sits in (0, 1] -- no zero
  division, no sign flip, no amplification.

# Exactness: the scale-invariance argument

The claim that CG's answer ignores the preconditioner has a rational
core one can state without any linear algebra: scaling M -> c M
(c > 0) scales z = M^-1 r by 1/c, and the iteration's outputs are
built from ratios in which the scale cancels. Concretely
(`Precond.lean`):

- `step_scale_invariant`: alpha d = (rz / dHd) d is unchanged when
  rz -> rz/c, dHd -> dHd/c^2, d -> d/c.
- `beta_scale_invariant`: beta = rz_next / rz is a ratio of two
  quantities scaling identically.
- `metric_update_scales`: the tracked M-norm products scale linearly,
  so the boundary comparison against a radius in the same metric is
  the same comparison.

The Rust test `nystrom_flattens_a_decaying_spectrum` then closes the
loop end to end: on a spectrum l_i = 1e4 / i^2 it requires the
preconditioned step to equal the plain step (exactness) and the
sketch's `k` actions plus the preconditioned solve to spend fewer
total actions than the plain solve (the clock actually sped up).

# Where randomization is refused

The same discipline says where not to randomize. The `par` feature's
host threading was measured 2.6x slower than serial at n = 20000 and
now sits behind a length floor; stochastic-dynamics noise inside an
acceptance chain is priced exponentially by the consumer's own
theorems (anneal's `shave_convicts`); and any preconditioner that is
not positive definite forfeits its metric, which `steihaug_pcg`
detects (rz <= 0) and answers with the safe steepest boundary step
rather than trusting a broken clock.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/scg.org`

Moller's scaled conjugate gradient (`src/scg.rs`) is the odd member of
the family: a conjugate-gradient method with no line search at all.
It is worth understanding as a one-dimensional trust region, because
that is what its damping parameter is.

# The step from a damped model

Along the current conjugate direction `d`, SCG builds the quadratic
model from the directional derivative mu = d . g and a curvature
estimate gamma ` d . H d, then damps the curvature with lambda >` 0:

  delta ` gamma + lambda norm(d)^2,     alpha ` -mu / delta.

The damping plays exactly the role of the trust radius: lambda = 0
trusts the quadratic model fully (a Newton-like step along the ray);
large lambda shrinks the step toward a small gradient step. After each
step the comparison ratio

  Delta = 2 (f(x + alpha d) - f(x)) / (alpha mu)

measures how quadratic the function actually was, and lambda is
lowered when the model earned trust (Delta large) and raised
fourfold when it did not -- the same shrink-grow policy as
`update_radius`, acting on stiffness instead of length.

# A bound on the step

A positive finite `Control::maxmove` bounds the Euclidean length of every trial step, retries included.
A bounded step is a fraction `t` of the model minimizer, and its ratio divides the measured change by the model change `alpha mu + alpha^2 delta / 2` instead of `alpha mu / 2`.
The formula above would overstate the agreement of such a step by the factor `2 - t`.
@@rst::doc:`Step bounds for log-hyperparameter fits <step-bounds>`@@ derives this and asks what fixes the size of the bound.

# Where the curvature comes from

The reference algorithm prices gamma with a one-sided finite
difference of gradients along `d`, one extra gradient per iteration.
When the objective implements `DirectionalCurvature` -- and via the
blanket impl, whenever it implements `HessianVector` -- the crate's
`minimize_scg_exact` replaces the probe with the exact action
d . H(x) d, the same Newton-Krylov pricing TAO's `nls` obtains from
user Hessian-vector callbacks. One trait method turns the probe cost
into an action cost; nothing else in the algorithm changes.

# Safeguards

A non-descent direction (mu >= 0) resets to steepest descent before
the step is priced -- conjugacy is a performance device, never a
correctness assumption. Non-finite trial values raise the damping and
retry within a fixed budget, and a probe that cannot find a finite
curvature reports `ScgStalled` rather than inventing one. The
convergence gate combines a step-size test in the infinity norm with
a relative objective test, both scaled, so neither a tiny step at a
steep point nor a flat stretch at a large step reads as convergence
alone.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/simd.org`

Contiguous `dot`, `sum`, `nrm2` (via `dot`), `axpy`, `scale`,
`mul_assign`, and `div_assign_floor` use one reduction shape.
`dot` keeps eight partials, `p0` through `p7`. Each product is one
`mul_add` into its partial, then `(p0+p4)`, `(p1+p5)`, `(p2+p6)`,
`(p3+p7)`, then one `mul_add` per tail element. `axpy` is
`a.mul_add(x, y)` per element. `sum` uses the same pair tree with
plain adds. The portable clone is that `mul_add` loop with no ISA
feature enabled. Hardware FMA rounds once, and so does `f64::mul_add`,
so the portable clone is the bit reference.

The `simd` feature compiles those loops with multiversion 0.9.
The clones are `x86_64+avx512f+fma` (rustc >= 1.89, `build.rs` cfg
`rgmin_avx512`), `x86_64+avx2+fma`, `aarch64+sve`, `aarch64+neon`, and
the default clone. Code outside the clones stays on the compiler
default, x86-64 and armv8-a. The build does not pass `-C target-cpu`
or `-march`. Selection is runtime. A CPU without a clone runs the
default clone. It does not execute that clone's instructions.

`RGMIN_SIMD` is read once, in the `OnceLock` that caches the override.
Accepted names are `scalar`, `avx2`, `avx512`, `neon`, and `sve`.
An unknown name is ignored. A known name this CPU cannot run selects
the portable path. The AVX2 clone requires FMA. A CPU with AVX2 and
no FMA stays on `mul_add`. A thread-local test override is read on
the calling thread before a rayon fan-out. Workers receive the path
that was chosen there. They do not call `getenv`.

The `par` feature keeps the same tree. The chunk length is 4096, a
multiple of 8, and does not depend on the pool size. Each contiguous
chunk is folded by the active kernel, and those totals are added from
the first index upward. Element updates use the same chunk length.
Lengths below 65536 stay serial. Thread count does not change a bit.
`dot_ordered` is a separate left fold of unfused products for noise
projections. It is not the eight-partial tree and it is not dispatched.

The same input, including -0.0, subnormals, 1 ulp values, and NaN
payloads, produces the same f64 bits on every clone and at 1, 2, 3,
and 8 threads. The SHA-256 of those bytes is `tests/golden/isa-hashes.toml`.
A clone the machine cannot execute is reported as not exercised.
The scalar path is always run by forcing it.

Páll and Hess, Comput. Phys. Commun. 184, 2641 (2013),
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpc.2013.06.003.
Dröge et al., Softw. Pract. Exp. 53, 176 (2023),
https://doi.org/10.1002/spe.3075.

`simd` is a default feature. The gate that decided that is in the
changelog. Default-on required a Holm-corrected wall-time ratio
interval below 1 on the atomistic bench or at n = 3e4, and no
micro-bench size slower beyond its interval.

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/step-bounds.org`

A Gaussian process (GP) fit by maximum a posteriori (MAP) often runs `minimize_scg` on log-hyperparameters.
This page states what a step bound does to scaled conjugate gradients (SCG), what the literature gives for its size, and which parts of a bound can be derived for those coordinates.

# What `maxmove` does in SCG

A positive finite `Control::maxmove` bounds the Euclidean length of every SCG trial step.
SCG computes `alpha = -mu / delta` along the direction `d`, with `mu = d . g`, `kappa = d . d` and the damped curvature `delta` of @@rst::doc:`scg <scg>`@@.
If `|alpha| sqrt(kappa)` exceeds the bound, `alpha` is scaled down so that the step has the bound as its length.
The same scaling applies at every retry after a non-finite trial.
A retry raises the damping from the same `mu`, and it can still ask for a long step.
Zero, negative, infinite and NaN values leave SCG unbounded.
Through the C ABI, zero and negative `maxmove` arrive as no bound.

# The comparison ratio for a bounded step

The damped model along `d` predicts the change `m(alpha) = alpha mu + alpha^2 delta / 2`.
Its minimizer `alpha* = -mu / delta` predicts `alpha* mu / 2`.
Moller's comparison ratio @@rst::cite:`mollerScaledConjugateGradient1993`@@ divides the measured change by that value.

#+begin_example
Delta = 2 (f(x + alpha d) - f(x)) / (alpha mu)
#+end_example

A bounded step is `alpha = t alpha*` with `0 < t < 1`.
Its model change is `alpha mu (1 - t / 2)`, so the formula above gives `2 - t` times the measured over predicted ratio.
With a tight bound the overstatement approaches a factor of 2.
The damping would then fall on an agreement as low as 0.375, where the 3/4 level calls for a fall only above 0.75.
SCG therefore divides a bounded step's measured change by `m(alpha)`, the ratio of Nocedal and Wright @@rst::cite:`nocedalNumericalOptimization2006`@@ eq. 4.4.
An unbounded step keeps the formula above.
Both forms give the ratio the same sign, so acceptance does not change.

# Why the per-atom 0.2 does not carry over

The default per-atom cap of 0.2 in rgmin 0.5.x cites the ASE `maxstep` and the eOn `maxMove`.
Both are atomic displacements, in the length unit of the geometry.
A log-hyperparameter has no unit, and a step of 0.2 in `log l` multiplies `l` by `exp(0.2) = 1.2214`.
The citation fixes a length, so it does not fix a step in these coordinates.

The cap also has the wrong shape there.
It bounds the largest Euclidean norm over consecutive `(x, y, z)` triples, so on five log-hyperparameters it bounds `||(d0, d1, d2)||_2` and `||(d3, d4)||_2`.
Which hyperparameters share a triple depends on the order in which the caller packs them, and no property of the fit fixes that grouping.

# What the literature gives

None of these sources sets a fixed per-step bound on log-hyperparameters.

- In the Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (GPML) toolbox, `minimize.m` starts along `-g` with a step of length `red |g| / (1 + |g|^2)`, at most 1/2 for the default `red = 1`.
  After that, the start of each line search may grow by up to a factor of 10 and its extrapolation by up to a factor of 3, with no fixed bound on the length.
- On a problem that is not fully boxed, L-BFGS-B @@rst::cite:`byrdLimitedMemoryAlgorithm1995`@@ takes a first step of length at most 1.
  After that, only the box limits the step.
- scikit-learn `GaussianProcessRegressor` runs L-BFGS-B on log-transformed parameters inside a box, `+-ln(1e5) = +-11.513` for the default length-scale bounds.
- GPstuff `fminscg` takes `alpha = -mu / delta` with no clip, from `sigma0 = 1e-4` and `lambda = 10`.
- The GP-NEB and GP-dimer papers of Koistinen et al. @@rst::cite:`koistinenNudgedElasticBand2017,koistinenNudgedElasticBand2019,koistinenMinimumModeSaddle2020`@@ and Goswami et al. @@rst::cite:`goswamiEfficientImplementationGaussian2025`@@ fit the hyperparameters by SCG with no step bound on them.
  Goswami and Jónsson @@rst::cite:`goswamiAdaptivePruningIncreased2026`@@ write in their optimal-transport GP paper that the hyperparameters have no direct physical reading.
- Nocedal and Wright @@rst::cite:`nocedalNumericalOptimization2006`@@ Algorithm 4.1 takes the overall bound as an input, and Theorems 4.5 and 4.6 converge for every positive value.
  Section 4.5 asks for a norm matched to how sensitive the model is to each variable.

So the theory leaves the value of the bound free.
The hyperparameters have no physical reading that could fix it.
The kernel still fixes the norm of the bound, and the likelihood fixes a unit for each variable.

# The shape from the kernel

Take the value block of the inverse-distance squared-exponential kernel of Koistinen et al. @@rst::cite:`koistinenNudgedElasticBand2019`@@, with `u_p = ln l_p` for pair type `p`:

#+begin_example
k ` sigma_c^2 + sigma_m^2 c,   c ` exp(-S / 2),   S ` sum_p s_p,   s_p ` Q_p exp(-2 u_p)
#+end_example

Here `Q_p >= 0` sums the squared differences of inverse distances of pair type `p`.

- Lemma 1 :: `dc / du_p = c s_p`.
- Lemma 2 :: `S exp(-S / 2) <= 2 / e = 0.735759` for `S >= 0`, with equality at `S = 2`.
- Theorem 1 :: A step `du` changes `c` to first order by at most `(2 / e) ||du||_inf`.
  The bound is sharp over all pairs of configurations.

The change is `c S sum_p (s_p / S) du_p`, a convex combination of the `du_p` times `S exp(-S / 2)`.
The bound is reached when all of `S` sits in the pair type with the largest `|du_p|` and `S = 2`.
So the steps whose worst first-order change of a correlation is at most `(2 / e) rho` form exactly the ball `||du||_inf <= rho`.
A Euclidean ball of radius `rho` lies inside it, and limits a step that moves all `m` coordinates alike to `rho / sqrt(m)` each.

- Theorem 2 :: For `||du||_inf <= rho`, the exact change of a correlation is at most `G(rho) = (1 - exp(-2 rho)) exp(-2 rho / (exp(2 rho) - 1))`, and the bound is reached.

`S` moves within `[S exp(-2 rho), S exp(2 rho)]`, and `exp(-S / 2)` is monotone, so the worst case is at an end of that range.
Maximizing over `S` gives `G`, which agrees with `2 rho / e` to first order and stays below it.

So `G` gives the worst case for each radius, and the kernel fixes the shape of the bound, the infinity norm.
It does not fix the radius.
Turning `G` into a radius needs a tolerance on the change of a correlation.
The problem does not supply one.

# A unit from the likelihood

The likelihood gives the Fisher information `F_ij = tr(K^-1 dK_i K^-1 dK_j) / 2` for `y ` N(0, K(theta))` with `n~ rows.

- Theorem 3 :: If `K = exp(v) C + B` with `C` and `B` positive semidefinite and free of `v = ln sigma_m^2`, then `F_vv <= n / 2`, with equality when `B = 0`.

`K^-1/2 exp(v) C K^-1/2` has its eigenvalues in `[0, 1]`, so `F_vv` is half a sum of `n` squares of numbers in that range.
The Cramer-Rao standard deviation of `ln sigma_m^2` is therefore at least `sqrt(2 / n)` for every kernel of that form and every system.
The constant term and the jitter make up `B` and only raise that floor.
For a length scale, `F_jj` depends on the data, and `1 / sqrt(F_jj)` is its Cramer-Rao standard deviation, with the other parameters known, once the fit computes it.

One standard deviation is the step at which the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence between the old and new models is about 1/2 nat.
That gives a candidate bound in the infinity norm: move each log-hyperparameter by at most its own standard deviation.
Without the data, only the signal variance has a known bound, `sqrt(2 / n)`, and using that radius for every coordinate is a further choice.
The choice of one standard deviation, rather than another multiple, is a choice of unit and not a theorem.

# Status

`minimize_scg` has no default bound, and the per-atom default of rgmin 0.5.x is not derived for log-hyperparameters.
The candidate above is not implemented and has not been tested on a GP-NEB run.
rgmin's step bounds are Euclidean or per triple, so a caller can only approach the infinity-norm shape from inside, with a Euclidean bound of the same radius.
Whether any of these radii gives a converged and certified path on a given system is an empirical question for the caller.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/explanation/trust-region.org`

Line searches commit to a direction and haggle over the length. Trust
regions invert the deal: fix a budget on the length, then ask for the
best step the local model affords inside it. This page derives the
machinery behind `src/trust.rs` (dense dogleg) and `src/hvp.rs`
(matrix-free Steihaug-Toint), and names the exact rational facts the
Lean proofs pin.

# The model and the ratio

Around the current point the quadratic model is

  m(p) = f + g . p + (1/2) p . H p,

trusted only within norm(p) <= Delta. After solving the subproblem
approximately for a step `p`, the honesty check compares the actual
reduction to the predicted one:

  rho = (f - f(x + p)) / (m(0) - m(p)).

The radius update (Nocedal-Wright algorithm 4.1, `update_radius`)
shrinks by four when rho < 1/4, doubles (capped) when rho > 3/4 and
the step pressed the boundary, and otherwise holds. Three properties
make this loop honest, each proved in
[proofs/lean/Rgmin/Trust.lean](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/blob/develop/proofs/lean/Rgmin/Trust.lean):

- `shrink_ge_floor` / `shrink_pos`: the radius never leaves the
  positive floor, so no division or comparison downstream degenerates.
- `shrink_strict` and the `collapse` recursion: consecutive failures
  decay the radius geometrically (one factor of four per rejection),
  so the loop must either accept a step or hit the floor in finitely
  many rejections -- at which point `minimize_newton_cg` returns the
  `TrustCollapsed` error instead of reporting convergence it does not
  have.
- `rejection_propagates`: with a positive predicted reduction, a step
  that failed to lower the objective has rho <= 0 < eta and cannot be
  accepted. The acceptance test cannot be talked into an uphill step
  by a large denominator.

# The value noise floor

The ratio needs the difference f - f(x + p) to carry information. A
value near 6e7 in double precision resolves differences of about
1e-8, so once the model predicts less than that, the numerator is
rounding and rho is noise. Every trial is then refused, the radius
decays by the `collapse` recursion, and the run ends in
`TrustCollapsed` with the gradient still above `gtol`, although
nothing is wrong with the model or the curvature action.

`NoiseFloor::with_eps_f` states the noise of the value, and
`minimize_newton_cg`, `minimize_newton_cg_precond` and the `newton-cg`
and `newton-pcg` sessions read it. When a trial is refused and the
model predicted a reduction of at most `c * eps_f`, the run stops at the
last accepted point with `Status::NoiseFloor`. A smaller radius only
lowers the predicted reduction, so no later trial from that point could
clear the noise either; the 24 shrinks from a unit radius to the floor
would buy nothing. A few units in the last place of the value is the
rounding noise of an objective summed in double precision.

The stop reports no convergence it does not have. The report carries
the gradient norm at that point, `converged` stays false unless the
norm is below `gtol`, and `Control::with_require_convergence` still
returns `Error::NotConverged`. No uphill step is taken: the test reads
only refused trials and leaves `reduction_ratio` and the acceptance
threshold alone. An accepted step whose predicted reduction is
under the noise does not stop the run. Without `eps_f` nothing
changes, and a collapse is still `TrustCollapsed`: that error keeps
meaning a non-finite gradient, a broken curvature action, or an
objective that rejects every trial for a reason the caller has not
named. Through the C ABI the field is `noise_eps_f` on
`rgmin_control_t` and the stop is `RGMIN_STOP_NOISE_FLOOR`, with `x`
holding the last accepted point.

# Steihaug-Toint: conjugate gradients under a leash

For large `n` the dense subproblem solve is the whole bill, so the
matrix-free path never forms `H`: it runs conjugate gradients on
H p = -g, spending one Hessian action per iteration, and stops early
on any of three events.

1. Small residual: the inexact-Newton forcing sequence
   rtol = min(sqrt(norm(g)), 1/2) keeps early outer iterations cheap and
   the tail superlinear (Nocedal-Wright eq. 7.3).
2. Negative curvature: if d . H d <= 0 the model is unbounded along
   `d`, and the right amount of greed is to walk the ray to the trust
   boundary. `Rgmin.ray_further_is_lower` in
   [Steihaug.lean](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/blob/develop/proofs/lean/Rgmin/Steihaug.lean)
   proves the model is nonincreasing along such a ray, so the boundary
   point minimizes the model on it.
3. Boundary crossing: if the next iterate would leave the region, the
   code solves for the exact crossing.

The crossing length `tau` is the positive root of

  dd tau^2 + 2 zd tau + (zz - r^2) = 0,

where zz, zd, dd are the tracked inner products of the current iterate
and direction. With the discriminant named as a square
(s^2 = zd^2 + dd (r^2 - zz)), two exact rational facts close the
construction, both in `Steihaug.lean`:

- `boundary_on_sphere`: the root lands exactly on the sphere,
  norm(z + tau d)^2 = r^2, in whichever inner product the caller
  tracked -- the same algebra serves the Euclidean and preconditioned
  runs.
- `boundary_tau_nonneg`: inside the region the root is nonnegative;
  a boundary exit extends the step, never retracts it.

The Rust test `negative_curvature_walks_to_the_trust_boundary` pins
the implemented step to the sphere at 1e-10 on an indefinite model.

# The metric bookkeeping under a preconditioner

`steihaug_pcg` runs the same loop under a preconditioner `M`, and the
trust boundary lives in the M-norm. The Conn-Gould-Toint recurrences
track p.Mp, p.Md, d.Md from quantities already on hand (with M z = r,
every needed product reduces to Euclidean dots), so norms cost no
extra applications of `M`. `Rgmin.metric_update_scales` in
[Precond.lean](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/rgmin/blob/develop/proofs/lean/Rgmin/Precond.lean) pins the
linearity that makes the tracked comparison scale-consistent, and the
Rust test `the_preconditioned_boundary_lives_in_the_sketch_metric`
holds the identity-preconditioner run bit-equal to the plain one.

# Dogleg, for when the Hessian is cheap

When a dense Hessian is affordable (`HessianObjective`), the dogleg
path (`dogleg_direction`) interpolates between the Cauchy point (the
model minimizer along -g) and the Newton point, taking whichever the
radius allows. It is the classical picture the Steihaug path
generalizes: CG's first iterate is the Cauchy step, its limit is the
Newton step, and truncation by the boundary lands in between.

# Newton and dogleg leave a saddle

A small force is not a positive Hessian, so dense Newton and dogleg
can stop on a first-order saddle. When the force is already under
`gtol`, the report reads the analytic Hessian before it returns.
The floor is max(abs(gtol), 1e-6, 1e-8 times the Frobenius norm of
H). A lowest eigenvalue below minus that floor is a kick: the step
is that mode, scaled so the largest per-atom displacement equals
the per-atom cap (`set_atom_maxmove`, or `istep` when the cap is
unset). At most four kicks in one solve. Each kick restarts the
dogleg radius at max(istep, 1e-8), the radius a new dogleg session
starts from. A lowest eigenvalue that is not below that floor still
evaluated the Hessian, so a converged Newton or dogleg report costs
one extra Hessian. `newton-cg` and `newton-pcg` do not take this
path, and neither does a HiGHS feasible set.

# Selecting it: `newton-cg` and `newton-pcg`

`Method::NewtonCg` (token `newton-cg`) and `Method::NewtonPcg`
(token `newton-pcg`) are session methods beside dense Newton and
dogleg. The string parser is `Method::from_name`; the C waist is
`rgmin_method_from_name`, with tokens `RGMIN_NEWTON_CG` and
`RGMIN_NEWTON_PCG`. `Solver::step` and `Solver::step_hess` on these
methods never call `hessian`. The product is analytic when the
caller uses `Solver::step_hvp` (or `minimize_method_hvp`), and a
forward difference of the known gradient otherwise: one extra
gradient per product, `h = 1e-8 / ||v||`. `Solver::try_step_hvp`
is that step when the host's callbacks return `Result`. The same
values, gradients and products take the same step. The first error is
`Error::Host`; nothing is evaluated after it, and `x` and the session
stay as they were before the step. A chart or distance
constraints on a Newton-CG or Newton-PCG session return
`Error::FallibleUnsupported`. `try_lowest_eigenpairs` and
`try_lowest_eigenpairs_precond` are the same split for one product.
`minimize_newton_cg_precond` runs the trust-region Newton-CG loop under a
caller `Preconditioner` in place of the identity; `minimize_newton_cg` is the
same loop with `IdentityPrecond`. The C entry is `rgmin_minimize_hvp_precond`.
The central-difference
wrapper `FdHvp` is unchanged and still costs two gradients; it is
not what the session uses.

`newton-pcg` rebuilds a rank-16 Nyström preconditioner
(Frangella, Tropp, Udell,
[10.1137/21M1466244](https://doi.org/10.1137/21M1466244)) at the
current point and runs `steihaug_pcg`. The subproblem boundary is
the preconditioner norm. If that step is longer than the Euclidean
radius, it is pulled back onto the Euclidean sphere before the
displacement cap. The trust ceiling stays Euclidean either way.

`control.maxmove` is that ceiling, the same rule as dogleg: when
it is unset the ceiling is eight times the current radius, and it
is never below the current radius. A per-atom cap
(`set_atom_maxmove`) clips only the accepted trial. The boundary
test that decides whether to double the radius uses the pre-clip
length, so a cap that shortens the trial does not freeze the
radius. Acceptance is rho > 1/10 (Nocedal-Wright), not dogleg's
rho > 0.

`Solver::gradient_calls` and `Solver::hvp_calls` accumulate for
the life of the session. `forget` does not clear them. A
forward-difference product is one `hvp_calls` entry, not a
gradient, so a harness charges `gradient_calls + hvp_calls` force
evaluations here and `n` force evaluations per dense Hessian on
Newton and dogleg.

Steihaug, /The Conjugate Gradient Method and Trust Regions in
Large Scale Optimization/, SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 20 (1983),
[10.1137/0720042](https://doi.org/10.1137/0720042).
Nocedal and Wright, /Numerical Optimization/, chapter 7,
[10.1007/978-0-387-40065-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-40065-5).

Source: `docs/orgmode/howto/ase-bench.org`

The median −0.012693 reported earlier for ASE LBFGS on LJ13 is not a
minimum. That start was a corner of a cubic lattice at spacing 1.5,
rattled by `Normal(0, 0.05)`. On seed 0, ASE LBFGS with its default
`alpha=70` (initial inverse Hessian `I/70`, longest atom at most 0.2)
does this:

| step | energy | max force | min pair | radius |
|------+------------+-----------+----------+--------|
| 0 | −7.044814 | 2.270844 | 1.3495 | 2.5068 |
| 1 | −4.571523 | 1.417897 | 1.5824 | 2.6311 |
| 31 | −0.023658 | 0.009242 | 3.0801 | 6.4782 |

The first step still moves inward. After that the radius grows on
every step and the force falls because the pairs have gone. The same
`alpha=70` on a compact 13-atom start stays bound, and `alpha=10` on
the cubic start is worse (energy +2448 after 80 steps). The lattice,
not the drop-in and not `alpha` by itself, is what produced −0.01.

The runs below do not use that lattice. LJ13 starts from the Mackay
icosahedron and LJ38 from the Oh truncated octahedron in the Cambridge
Cluster Database
(`https://www-wales.ch.cam.ac.uk/`jon/structures/LJ/points/13~ and
`.../38`). The database energies are −44.326801 and −173.928427. With
ASE's Lennard-Jones calculator (`epsilon = 1`, `sigma = 1`, `rc = 10`,
potential shifted to zero at the cutoff) those geometries evaluate to
−44.326489 and −173.925615. Ten seeds add `Normal(0, 0.05)` from
`PCG64(20261113 + seed)`. A second set draws points uniformly in a
sphere of density 1 with no pair closer than 0.9. Cu64 is unchanged:
fcc `a=3.615` repeated `(4, 4, 4)`, rattled the same way.

A run is converged only when the maximum force is below 0.01 eV/Å and
the largest distance from the centroid stays under twice the start
value. The other count is dissociations. Medians below are over the
converged runs. `ase-lbfgs` uses `alpha=70`. `ase-lbfgs-a10` uses
`alpha=10`.

rgmin FIRE is Bitzek's velocity-Verlet step: the force is mixed after
the move. The parameters are ASE's defaults (`dt=0.1`, `dtmax=1`,
`Nmin=5`, `finc=1.1`, `fdec=0.5`, `astart=0.1`, `fa=0.99`) and the
longest atom moves at most 0.2. ASE FIRE mixes before the Euler kick
and caps the Euclidean length of the whole displacement.
