| Morse Pt256 | capped session | 11 | 4.965 | 3.94e-3 | -1396.173 |

The chained Rosenbrock function
`sum_i (1 - x_i)^2 + 100 (x_{i+1} - x_i^2)^2` has a local minimum
for every `n >= 4` in the basin of `(-1, 1, ..., 1)`.
SciPy BFGS started at that point converges with a positive definite
Hessian. For `n = 4` the value is 3.701 and the first coordinate
is −0.776. For `n = 10` the value is 3.987 and the first coordinate
is −0.993, near `(-1, 1, ..., 1)` with value about 3.98.
For `n = 3` that start falls through to the valley floor at 0.
A step that stops at this local minimum has converged.
From the alternating start `(-1.2, 1, -1.2, 1, ...)` the capped
step enters that minimum for `n = 10` and `n = 100`, while the
Wolfe search and the geometry step reach value 0.
On LJ7 and LJ13, at an atomic force of 0.01, the geometry step
uses fewer evaluations and finishes at the same energy. On LJ38
the capped session uses 187 evaluations against 211 and finishes
about 4.3 energy units higher, in another basin. On the periodic
Morse cluster both session arms take 11 evaluations and the same
energy. The cap is the default because the eOn client does not
line-search this step. The fifty-start comparison is
`benches/ase_h2h/distribution.md`.

The same fmax and the same maxstep against ASE 3.29.0 are recorded
in `benches/ase_h2h/results.md`.

## Newton and RFO when the Hessian is cheap

L-BFGS is the production method when only `f` and `∇f` are available.
When a dense Hessian is cheap (analytic pair potential, model Hessian),
the direction is a Newton step, not a two-loop pair history.

- Banerjee, Adams, Simons, Shepard 1985 is rational function
  optimization
  ([10.1021/j100247a015](https://doi.org/10.1021/j100247a015)).
- Baker 1986 is the restricted-step form used in geometry codes
  ([10.1002/jcc.540070402](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.540070402)).
- Nocedal and Wright, chapter 3 / 6, record the Levenberg-shifted
  Newton step `(H + μ I)^{-1} g`.

`Method::newton(NewtonKind::Shifted | NewtonKind::Rfo)` and
`minimize_newton` are that solver. The C waist is
`rgmin_minimize_hess`. It is not an L-BFGS option.

**Failure audit (12 agents per method)**

| method | Borda | Class | Evidence |
|---+---|---|---|
| SO(3) | 11/12 crash bug | `n!=9` is `Error::ManifoldDim` | `so3.rs` `required_dim`; `pack` is never called on 3N |
| SE(3) | 10/12 contract | `n!=12` is `Error::ManifoldDim` | `se3.rs` exact-12; no 9-prefix |
| sphere | 12/12 misuse | impl correct, `S^{3N-1}` | `sphere.rs:22-39`; cluster not on the unit sphere |
| Stiefel | 12/12 alias | `St(n,1)` = sphere | `stiefel.rs:11-23`; `stiefel_p` is always 1 |
| HiGHS | 9/12 wrong QP | `step_hess` solves dense Newton QP | `session.rs:322-336`; Morse `n=768` times out |
| PSO | 10/12 wrong tool | swarm on `[-1e12,1e12]` | `oracle.rs` unbounded; `230021 = 10000 x `23~ |
| SR2 | fixed | Powell symmetric Broyden in the SR1 trust region | `qn.rs` `sr2_hessian_update` |
| model Hessians | 11/12 wrong chemistry | covalent `B^T k B` vs pair | pair is the rematch `P` |

SO(3) and SE(3) reject a 3N cluster. Sphere/Stiefel on 3N stay
on `S^{3N-1}` and die on maxiter. Isolated molecules use
`rigid_quotient` or `mw_rigid`. PSO force
counts match `max_iterations` (10000 LJ38 / 1000 Morse) times
swarm work, not a 230x230 product. SR2 is Powell's symmetric Broyden
update in the SR1 trust region; the old rank-1 map failed the secant
condition.

## FIRE, Barzilai–Borwein, and dogleg

These four tokens share `rgmin_solver_t` and a fused `(f, g)`.

- FIRE (Bitzek 2006,
  [10.1103/PhysRevLett.97.170201](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.97.170201)) is the ASE / LAMMPS / eOn
  inertial stepper. One fused force per geometry.
- FIRE 2.0 (Guénolé 2020,
  [10.1016/j.commatsci.2020.109584](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.commatsci.2020.109584)) uses semi-implicit Euler:
  update velocity, mix it toward the force, then update position.  On
  non-positive power it applies the paper's half-step-back correction;
  a nonzero correction gets a fresh force before the forward step.
  The initial delay leaves the time step unchanged during the first
  delay window, and a clipped forward move rescales the stored velocity
  to the displacement actually taken.  More than 2,000 consecutive
  non-positive-power steps terminate as a stalled solve. An installed
  exponential preconditioner leaves that order in place and uses `P`
  as the metric: power is `F · v`, and the kick and the mix use
  `P^{-1} F`.
- `FirePreset::Guenole2020` (`set_fire_preset`, opt-in) takes
  Guenole 2020 Table 1 (arXiv:1908.02038v4, page 7), the LAMMPS
  `min_modify` defaults: `tmax` 10 and `tmin` 0.02 times the start
  step, `delaystep` 20, `dtgrow` 1.1, `dtshrink` 0.5, `alpha0` 0.25,
  `alphashrink` 0.99, `vdfmax` 2000, half step back and initial
  delay on, semi-implicit Euler. A shrink that would pass `dt_min`
  keeps `dt` (Algorithm 2, line 23). The default set has
  `dt_max = 2.5 istep`, `dt_min = 1e-12`, `N_delay = 5` and
  `alpha_start = 0.1`, and clamps the shrink at `dt_min`.
  Under the preset or ABC the session keeps its velocity unless a
  cap or a bound moved the trial, since `(x + dx - x) / dt` rounds
  `v` by about `u |x| / |dx|`.
- ABC-FIRE is the accelerated bias-corrected (ABC) update of
  Echeverri Restrepo and Andric 2023
  ([10.1016/j.commatsci.2022.111978](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.commatsci.2022.111978)).
  The opt-in setter `set_fire_abc` turns it on for `fire2` only.
  The update sets `alpha` to at least `1e-10` before the mix. It then
  divides the mixed velocity by `1 - (1 - alpha)^(N+1)`, where `N` is
  the count of consecutive positive-power steps. Each velocity
  component is then clipped to the cap over `dt`, and the cap
  bounds each displacement component. This follows ASE 3.30.0b1
  `ase/optimize/fire2.py` (`use_abc`). LAMMPS `src/min_fire.cpp`
  (commit `9ce13d52`) uses the same floor and clip, with exponent
  `ntimestep - last_negative`, one less than ASE.
- `src/fire.rs` replays ASE `FIRE2` on the extended Rosenbrock
  function (`tests/ase_fire2_gold.py`) one step at a time, with and
  without ABC. ASE has neither the initial delay nor `vdfmax` and
  clamps the shrink, so the script checks that power stays positive
  for the first 20 steps and that no shrink reaches `dt_min`.
- Barzilai–Borwein (1988,
  [10.1093/imanum/8.1.141](https://doi.org/10.1093/imanum/8.1.141)) with Raydan's nonmonotone globalization
  ([10.1137/S1052623494266365](https://doi.org/10.1137/S1052623494266365)) is a two-point spectral step.
- Powell dogleg (Nocedal–Wright algorithm 4.1) consumes the host
  pair Hessian already passed to `rgmin_solver_step_hess`.
- Steihaug–Toint Newton-CG (`newton-cg`, and `newton-pcg` with a
  rank-16 Nyström preconditioner) is a session method. Hessian
  access is a product: analytic through `step_hvp`, otherwise one
  forward difference of the gradient. `maxmove` is the Euclidean
  trust ceiling; a per-atom cap clips the trial only.
  Steihaug 1983
  ([10.1137/0720042](https://doi.org/10.1137/0720042)),
  Nocedal–Wright chapter 7.

ARC, DFP, SPSA, CMA-ES, Nelder–Mead, and BOBYQA were surveyed and
not added: DFP is dominated by BFGS already in the crate, and the
derivative-free methods waste force calls on an analytic PES.

## Nonlinear CG

Hager and Zhang 2005 (`CG_DESCENT`)
([10.1137/030601880](https://doi.org/10.1137/030601880)) is the cheapest NLCG on this protocol
(13859 / 5336) and does not beat rematch L-BFGS.

## Embedded manifolds

The session retracts onto an embedded manifold when the host
asks. The geometry is manopt_cpp `proj` / `retr` / `transp` on a
rank-1 f64 vector.

- Absil, Mahony, Sepulchre 2008 is the matrix-manifold
  reference
  ([10.1515/9781400830244](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400830244)).
- Riemannian conjugate gradients use that retraction and that transport.
  The transport is scaled when the image is longer than the vector it carried (Ring and Wirth 2012, [10.1137/11082885X](https://doi.org/10.1137/11082885X); Sato and Iwai 2015, [10.1080/02331934.2013.836650](https://doi.org/10.1080/02331934.2013.836650); Sato 2016, [10.1007/s10589-015-9801-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10589-015-9801-1); Sato 2022, [10.1007/978-3-030-62391-3](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-62391-3)).
- Boumal 2023 is the smooth-manifold course
  ([10.1017/9781009166164](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009166164)).
- Manopt (Boumal, Mishra, Absil, Sepulchre 2014) is the
  factory contract this crate ports
  ([JMLR 15, 1455 (2014)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/boumal14a.html)).
- ROPTLIB (Huang, Absil, Gallivan, Hand 2018) is the C++
  library that names Stiefel and SE(3) in the same waist
  ([10.1145/3218822](https://doi.org/10.1145/3218822)).

`minimize_rlbfgs` is cautious limited-memory Riemannian BFGS,
Algorithm 2 of Huang, Absil, and Gallivan 2018
([10.1137/17M1127582](https://doi.org/10.1137/17M1127582)).
The two-loop map is Huang, Gallivan, and Absil 2015
([10.1137/140955483](https://doi.org/10.1137/140955483)).
On Euclidean space the transport is the identity and the update is
the cautious BFGS method of Li and Fukushima 2001
([10.1137/S1052623499354242](https://doi.org/10.1137/S1052623499354242)).
The section 7 choices are memory 4, `vartheta(t) = 10^{-4} t`, an
Armijo–Goldstein backtrack from a unit trial, and the stop
`||g_f|| / ||g_0|| < 10^{-6}`. The vector transport is the parallel
transport of the exponential when that pair exists. This is not the
sphere great-circle search, and the default Euclidean L-BFGS step
stays the eOn cap.

Euclidean is the default. An isolated molecule uses
`RigidQuotient` (`R^{3N}/SE(3)`; Sella Cartesian
`fix_translation` / `fix_rotation`,
doi:10.1021/acs.jctc.2c00395) or `MwRigid` (Page–McIver
mass-weighted Eckart, doi:10.1063/1.454172). Sphere, SO(3) as a
9-vector, Stiefel `St(n,1)`, SE(3) as a 12-vector, and SPD as
an n² row-major matrix are matrix-manifold embeddings and
reject a 3N cluster.

## Defaults in this crate

- Method: `Lbfgs` / `Method::lbfgs_with_memory(8)`, line-search-free
  cap `EON_MAX_MOVE` (0.2)
- Opt-in line search: `LbfgsStep::Wolfe`, constants `c1 = 1e-4`,
  `c2 = 0.9`, at most 20 trials
- First trial of that search: `1` when the memory is occupied;
  the initial step length when the memory is empty
- Relative-decrease stop: off on `Lbfgs` (`ftol: 0.0`);
  `LBFGSB_FTOL` is the SciPy L-BFGS-B default
- Gradient stop: `norminf(g) < 1e-6` on `Lbfgs`, `norm2(g)` on
  `minimize_lbfgs` so existing cold-start reports stay comparable
- Session stop: `norm2(g) < gtol` by default. `Control::stop_norm`
  or `Solver::set_stop_norm` selects the largest per-atom norm (ASE
  `fmax`, eOn `max_atom`, LAMMPS `max`), the largest component (eOn
  `max_component`, LAMMPS `inf`) or `norm2(g) / sqrt(n)` (eOn `rms`)

## A-posteriori nonlinear certificates

`certificate` combines caller-supplied majorants in standard `f64`
floating-point arithmetic without outward rounding:

- `kantorovich_ball` evaluates the classical Newton--Kantorovich
  existence radius `2 eta / (1 + sqrt(1 - 2 h))` under `h <= 1/2`
  (Kantorovich and Akilov 1982,
  [10.1016/B978-0-08-023036-8.50024-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-023036-8.50024-2); Gragg and Tapia 1974,
  [10.1137/0711002](https://doi.org/10.1137/0711002)) @@rst::cite:`kantorovichNewtonsMethod1982,graggOptimalErrorBounds1974`@@.
  Because `r <= 2 eta` whenever `h <= 1/2`, an induced operator-norm
  Lipschitz bound for `J` on `B(x0, 2 eta)` suffices.
- `adjoint_functional_bar` adds the dual-weighted residual
  `first_order = |lambda^T F(x0)|` for an exact adjoint
  `J(x0)^T lambda = grad q(x0)` to the nonlinear displacement and
  quadratic Taylor remainders, using the dual norm for `grad q(x0)`
  and the induced operator norm for `D^2 q` (Becker and Rannacher
  2001, [10.1017/S0962492901000010](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0962492901000010))
  @@rst::cite:`beckerOptimalControlApproach2001`@@.
- `certify_morse_gap` certifies that a projected self-adjoint operator
  cannot cross zero inside the Kantorovich ball by Weyl's eigenvalue
  perturbation inequality (Weyl 1912,
  [10.1007/BF01456804](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01456804))
  @@rst::cite:`weylAsymptotischeVerteilungsgesetzEigenwerte1912`@@,
  requiring `operator_lipschitz` to bound the spectral-norm Lipschitz
  constant of the operator.

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/bfgs.org`

# BFGS

Dense BFGS keeps an inverse Hessian, starting from the identity. Himmelblau has four minima. From `(0, 0)` the session reaches `(3.584, -1.848)`, not `(3, 2)`.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_bfgs.rs`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it builds.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_bfgs.rs`

ASE's `BFGS` multiplies the first step by `1/alpha` with `alpha = 70`. This session does not. The EMT gold in `python/tests/test_ase_optimizer.py` checks the minimum, not that first step.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/cg.org`

# Conjugate gradients

Two steps share the Polak-Ribière coefficient. `Method::eon_cg` is that coefficient with the Powell restart at 0.5, and the session still line-searches. `minimize_eon_cg` is the client step: one curvature probe, no line search, then the per-atom cap.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_cg.rs`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it builds.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_cg.rs`

`Method::polak_ribiere_plus` is SciPy's `method="CG"`: `max(0, β)`. The Python session named `cg` uses that coefficient with a strong Wolfe search, because SciPy does. The eOn client step does not.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/eigenpairs.org`

# Lowest eigenpairs

`lowest_eigenpairs` is block LOBPCG for the k lowest pairs of a symmetric product (Knyazev 2001). The caller supplies `H(x) v`. The seed block has shape `(n, k)`. Values come back ascending, and the vectors are the columns of an `(n, k)` array, with the residual norm and a converged flag for each pair. A pair that misses the tolerance raises `RuntimeError` unless `strict=False`.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_lowest_eigenpairs.py`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it runs.

`lowest_eigenpairs` is in the maturin package under `python/`, which is not on PyPI. Install it with `python -m pip install './python'` from a checkout, as @@rst::doc:`../howto/install`@@ shows. The PyPI wheel does not have it.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_lowest_eigenpairs.py`

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/fire.org`

# FIRE

`Method::fire(FireKind::V2)` is FIRE 2.0. `Solver::set_fire_preset(FirePreset::Guenole2020)` installs the published parameter set. `FireConfig::ase` is the ASE constructor (`dtmax = 1`) rather than the session default `dt_max = 2.5 dt`.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_fire.rs`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it builds.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_fire.rs`

The Python class `rgmin.FIRE` passes the ASE arguments (`dt`, `dtmax`, `Nmin`, `finc`, `fdec`, `astart`, `fa`) into `FireConfig`.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/lbfgs-direction.org`

# One L-BFGS direction with your own H0

`LbfgsPairs` is the two-loop recursion with the pair memory handed to the caller. It returns the direction `-H g` for a gradient you supply and does not evaluate an objective, so a host that has its own step rule, line search or preconditioner can use the L-BFGS metric alone.

The starting matrix `H0` is the argument of `LbfgsPairs::direction`, and it takes three forms of `LbfgsH0`: `Scale(gamma)` is `gamma I`, `Diagonal(d)` is one entry per coordinate, and `Apply(f)` is a callback `v -> H0 v` that runs once, on the vector in the middle of the two loops.

The example first checks the empty memory, where the direction is `-gamma g`. It then pushes one pair, compares the direction with the one `Lbfgs::two_loop` gives for the same pair, and finishes by checking that a diagonal and the callback that applies it agree.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_lbfgs_direction.rs`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it builds.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_lbfgs_direction.rs`

`LbfgsPairs::push` returns `Ok(true)` when it stored the pair. A pair that fails the relative-curvature test is dropped and the call returns `Ok(false)`, which is not an error.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/lbfgs.org`

# L-BFGS

The default step is the eOn cap. The longest atom moves by at most 0.2, the first step probes curvature, and a proposal that long clears the memory. `Lbfgs::builder().wolfe()` is the strong Wolfe search. `Lbfgs::scaled` is the ASE length control: shorten the step and keep the pairs.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_lbfgs.rs`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it builds.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_lbfgs.rs`

On the 10-dimensional Rosenbrock start, that cap reaches the minimum at 0. The ASE scale stops in the well near `x0 = -1`, where the infinity norm is already below `1e-5` and the value is about 4. `tests/scaled_rosenbrock10.rs` is that comparison. SciPy's L-BFGS-B also reaches 0; the difference is the step rule.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/linesearch.org`

# A line search on values you already have

A host that owns the potential cannot hand it to a library: it counts every force call itself, and a second call inside the optimizer would spoil the count.
`SuppliedSearch` turns the search around. The host passes the energy and gradient at the start, then at each trial the search names, and the search says either "evaluate here next" or "accepted". It never calls an objective.

The search constants are the strong Wolfe ones, `LineSearch::wolfe(c1, c2, maxiter)` with `c1 < c2`. The example runs `LineSearch::search` on a closure first, then drives `SuppliedSearch` over the same function, and asserts that the two accept the same step length and the same point. @@rst::doc:`../explanation/linesearch`@@ explains the rules.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_linesearch.rs`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it builds.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_linesearch.rs`

The same loop is the C entry `rgmin_linesearch` and the Python class `rgmin.LineSearch` of the maturin package.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/manifold-fit.org`

# Fit a point on St x SPD

This tutorial fits a frame `U` on `St(6, 2)` and a matrix `S` on `SPD(3)` to a target `(U*, S*)` by Riemannian gradient steps.
The cost is `f(U, S) = |U - U*|^2 / 2 + |S - S*|^2 / 2`, so the Euclidean gradient is `(U - U*, S - S*)`.

The program is `examples/tutorial_manifold_fit.py`. Continuous integration runs it.

`Product`, `Stiefel` and `SPD` are in the maturin package under `python/`, which is not on PyPI. Install it with `python -m pip install './python'` from a checkout, as @@rst::doc:`../howto/install`@@ shows. The PyPI wheel does not have them.

Build the product once. `"polar"` selects the second-order Stiefel retraction, and the SPD factor uses the affine-invariant metric.

```python
from rgmin import SPD, Product, Stiefel

manifold = Product(Stiefel(6, 2, "polar"), SPD(3, "affine_invariant"))
```

A point is a tuple `(U, S)` of a `(6, 2)` and a `(3, 3)` array.
Each step converts the Euclidean gradient to the Riemannian gradient and retracts `-t` times it.

```python
for _ in range(200):
    egrad = (x[0] - target[0], x[1] - target[1])
    rgrad, x = manifold.gradient_step(x, egrad, 0.1)
```

The script asserts that the cost falls at every step, that `U^T U = I` to `1e-12`, that `S` stays positive definite, and that the final cost is below a thousandth of the first.
The affine-invariant gradient is `S sym(G) S`, so it grows with the eigenvalues of `S`; the fixed step `0.1` suits a target whose eigenvalues are of order one.
`manifold.norm(x, rgrad)` is the Riemannian length of the last gradient.

The same step from C is `rgmin_manifold_gradient_step` on a handle from `rgmin_manifold_product`, with `U` and `S` packed column-major one after the other.
@@rst::doc:`../reference/manifold`@@ lists every operation.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/migration.org`

# From ASE, SciPy and eOn

The Rust default is the eOn L-BFGS cap (`EON_MAX_MOVE = 0.2`), not a line search. `LbfgsStep::Wolfe` opts into strong Wolfe. `LbfgsStep::Scaled` is ASE `LBFGS` with `use_line_search=False`: shorten the step, keep the pairs.

| Call site | rgmin |
| ASE `BFGS(atoms, trajectory=, logfile=)` | `rgmin.BFGS`. The initial Hessian is the identity, not `alpha * I`. |
| ASE `LBFGS(..., use_line_search=False)` | `rgmin.LBFGS`. Same length control. |
| ASE `LBFGS(..., use_line_search=True)` | `rgmin.LBFGS(use_line_search=True)`, the strong Wolfe search. |
| ASE `FIRE(dt=, dtmax=, Nmin=, finc=, fdec=, astart=, fa=)` | `rgmin.FIRE`. `dtmax` is kept. A Rust session would use `2.5 * dt`. |
| eOn `opt_method = lbfgs`, `max_move = 0.2` | `Lbfgs::default` or `rgmin.LBFGS(eon_cap=True)`. |
| eOn `cg` | `minimize_eon_cg`. `Method::eon_cg` is only the coefficient and the restart. |
| SciPy `method="L-BFGS-B"` | `Lbfgs::minimize_box` for bounds. `LBFGSB_FTOL` is SciPy's `ftol`. The stop there is the projected gradient. |
| SciPy `method="CG"` | `Method::polak_ribiere_plus`, `max(0, β)`. |

`run(fmax, steps)`, `attach`, `trajectory` and `logfile` are ASE's. The classes subclass `ase.optimize.optimize.Optimizer`.

The scaled step is not the one to copy when the function has a flat well. On the 10-dimensional Rosenbrock start, ASE's length control stops near `x0 = -1` with value about 4 and an infinity norm below `1e-5`. The eOn cap and the Wolfe search both reach the minimum at 0. SciPy's L-BFGS-B does too. `tests/scaled_rosenbrock10.rs` and `python/tests/test_ase_optimizer.py` record that. The tolerance is the same; the step rule is what leaves the well.

`Stepper::step` is the one-iteration seam rgsaddle already calls on `Solver`.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/newton.org`

# A quadratic in Python

Install the package from PyPI, then minimize
\(f(x) = \tfrac12 x \cdot x\).

```bash
python -m pip install rgmin
```

A checkout that can build the Rust static library installs the same
package with `python -m pip install .` from the repository root.

```python
import numpy as np
import rgmin

def f_and_grad(x):
    return 0.5 * float(x @ x), np.array(x, copy=True)

x0 ` np.array([1.0, -2.0, 0.5], dtype`np.float64)
report, x ` rgmin.minimize(f_and_grad, x0, method`"lbfgs", gtol=1e-12)
assert report.grad_norm < 1e-8
```

`x0` has to be a contiguous float64 array. The same array is updated
in place, and `minimize` also returns it.

One iteration at a time uses a solver:

```python
config ` rgmin.SolverConfig("lbfgs", memory`20)
solver = rgmin.Solver(x0.shape[0], config)
report = solver.step(f_and_grad, x0)
```

ASE is a separate install, `python -m pip install 'rgmin[ase]'`.
`import rgmin` does not import ASE.

# Quickstart

This tutorial minimizes the 2-D Rosenbrock banana from the classic start `(-1.2, 1.0)` with the default L-BFGS step, the line-search-free cap of 0.2.

## What you will need

Rust 1.88 or newer, and a new Cargo project with the release from crates.io:

```bash
cargo new rosenbrock
cd rosenbrock
cargo add rgmin@0.8 ndarray@0.17 eindir-core@0.6
```

Each sample below is a whole program. Put it in `src/main.rs` and run it with `cargo run`.
The same programs are `examples/tutorial_quickstart.rs` and `examples/tutorial_session.rs` in the repository, and continuous integration runs both.

To follow the `develop` branch instead, take rgmin from git as @@rst::doc:`../howto/install`@@ shows.
`eindir-core` 0.6 still comes from crates.io, so the samples below compile on either route.

## Rust

A closure is enough.
The stepper does not care who owns the potential.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_quickstart.rs`

## Session

Hosts that already own an outer loop hold a `Solver` and call `step` once per iteration.
The host also decides when to stop, here when the gradient norm drops below 1e-4:

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_session.rs`

`Accept::Energy` makes each step refuse a rise in the energy.
The default, `Accept::None`, takes every step without that check, for hosts that have forces but no energy.
The session uses the same line-search-free cap unless the caller sets `LbfgsStep::Wolfe`.

@@rst::doc:`Relax a platinum crystal <relax-morse>`@@ runs that loop to convergence on a 256-atom system.

@@rst::doc:`Retract onto an embedded manifold <../howto/manifolds>`@@ shows how `set_manifold` keeps each step on a sphere, a rigid-body quotient or another set.

## What just happened

1. `Lbfgs::minimize` ran the two-loop recursion on the Rosenbrock banana from `(-1.2, 1.0)`.
2. The closure returned `(f, g)`; the crate never needed a named potential type.
3. The `Solver` session took one step per call, refused any step that raised the energy, and left the stop test to the caller.

# Riemannian conjugate gradients

`minimize_rcg` runs Fletcher-Reeves, PRP+ @@rst::cite:`Gilbert_1992`@@ or Hager-Zhang on a manifold the crate already retracts.
The vector transport is that manifold's, scaled back to its original length when the image is longer (Sato and Iwai, [10.1080/02331934.2013.836650](https://doi.org/10.1080/02331934.2013.836650)).
`RcgTransport::Identity` is the Euclidean case.
The default line search is strong Wolfe with curvature constant 0.1.
`LineSearch::default` selects Brent instead.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_rcg.rs`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it builds.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_rcg.rs`

The example calls `minimize_rcg` on a quadratic and checks both coordinates.

`RcgOptions::validate` refuses a gradient tolerance that is not finite or is negative, and an initial step that is not finite and positive, with `Error::InvalidControl`.
`minimize_rcg` calls it before the first evaluation.
A projection or retraction that cannot be carried out is returned as its typed error rather than skipped.
A start off the manifold is retracted by a zero step, so the run begins on the manifold.

## In a session

`Method::rcg()` runs the same step inside a `Solver`.
There it keeps the session's rules:

- `Control::maxmove` and the per-atom cap bound the move that is taken.
  A trial beyond a cap lies outside the line-search domain, so the search contracts to the cap.
  The default per-atom cap stays off for this method.
- A distance constraint set composes with the configured manifold.
  The tangent space is the intersection of the manifold's and the bonds', and the retraction alternates between the two until both hold.
  A set with masses steps along the cut gradient raised by the inverse masses, which is tangent to the bonds, and its line search measures that direction in the mass metric.
- The stop and the report read the gradient cut by the bonds, so a constrained minimum with a pure constraint force meets the tolerance.
  A start that misses its bonds is retracted onto them first, so a reported tolerance holds at a point that keeps every bond.
- A level-set retraction that moves the point clears the held direction.
  The next step opens on steepest descent.
- The step and the stop read the session's field.
  The gradient, the tangent projection and the transport are the session's: on a rigid quotient, a product with rigid blocks, or a periodic session they carry the session masses, the periodic flag and the removal of the declared rigid motion.
  The conjugacy coefficient and the stop are formed in that field.
  A distance constraint set with masses is the exception: its step follows the cut gradient raised by the inverse masses, while the stop and the report read the cut gradient.
- A start off the manifold is projected onto it, as `minimize_rcg` does with a zero retraction, so the first evaluation, the held value and the point handed back are on the manifold.
  A zero-budget run judges the start at that same point.
  Nothing is refused for it.
- Every trial stays in the objective's box and on the manifold.
  Where the manifold fills the ambient coordinates, the trial is the retraction clipped to the box, which is the projection onto that intersection.
  On every other manifold the trial is the retraction of a tangent step in the box's tangent cone, and a retraction that would leave the box is refused so the search shortens.
  A start with no retraction in the box returns `Error::OffManifold` before the objective reads a point.
  So does a start that a distance constraint set moves out of the box when it puts the start on its bonds.
- Each Wolfe slope is the derivative of the value along the curve that is walked: the Euclidean gradient against the curve velocity.
  It does not go through `Manifold::inner`, so a manifold whose `inner` is not the metric of its Riemannian gradient still gets the strong Wolfe tests.
  The norms, the transport scaling and the conjugacy coefficient do read `Manifold::inner`, which is the conformal metric on the Poincare ball and the Minkowski form on the hyperboloid.
- A step whose best finite decrease misses the energy noise of `NoiseFloor::with_eps_f` keeps its start and reports `Status::NoiseFloor`, as the other methods do.
  The direction and step memory are the ones held at that start, not the ones the step built at the refused point.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/relax-morse.org`

# Relax a platinum crystal with L-BFGS and FIRE

This tutorial relaxes 256 platinum atoms in a periodic box with three methods from `rgmin`: limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (L-BFGS) @@rst::cite:`liuLimitedMemoryBfgs1989`@@, the fast inertial relaxation engine (FIRE) @@rst::cite:`bitzekStructuralRelaxationMade2006`@@, and FIRE 2.0 @@rst::cite:`guenoleAssessmentOptimizationFast2020`@@.
At the end you have the relaxed energy from each method and a plot of how many force calls each one needed.

## What you will need

- A checkout of `rgmin` and Rust 1.88 or newer.
- Python 3 with matplotlib, only to redraw the figure.

## The system

The start is `tests/data/morse_pos_0000.con`: 256 Pt atoms in a cubic cell of side 16.387907 Å.
The atoms interact through a Morse pair potential with \(D_0 ` 0.7102\) eV, \(\alpha ` 1.6047\) Å^{-1}, and \(r_0 = 2.897\) Å, cut at 7.0 Å and shifted to zero there, the same potential the Morse tests use.
At the start the energy is -1392.989740 eV and the largest force on any atom is 1.556715 eV/Å.

## Run the example

```bash
cargo run --release --example relax_morse > trace.csv
```

The program prints one line per method when it stops:

#+begin_example
lbfgs: 9 steps, 11 force calls, E ` -1396.173007 eV, fmax ` 0.006474 eV/Å
fire: 50 steps, 51 force calls, E ` -1396.172302 eV, fmax ` 0.009318 eV/Å
fire2: 42 steps, 46 force calls, E ` -1396.172349 eV, fmax ` 0.009145 eV/Å
#+end_example

`trace.csv` holds one row per step: method, step, force calls so far, energy, and the largest per-atom force.
Row 0 is the start.

## How the loop works

#+CAPTION: The host owns the loop, and one step may ask for several force calls.
[[file:../../figures/relax-morse/session_loop.png]]

The example never hands the whole job to the library.
It builds a `Solver` session, then calls `step` until the force is small enough, the way a geometry host such as eOn drives an optimizer.
This is the core of `examples/relax_morse.rs` with the printing left out:

```rust
let mut solver = Solver::new(method, control, x0.len());
solver.set_atom_maxmove(0.2);
solver.set_stop_norm(StopNorm::MaxAtom);

let mut x = x0.clone();
while steps < BUDGET && last >= FMAX {
    let rep = solver.step(&obj, &mut x).expect("step");
    steps += 1;
    last = rep.grad_norm;
}
```

`obj` is an `Oracle` around a closure that returns the energy and its gradient and adds one to a counter on every call.
`set_atom_maxmove` caps how far any atom moves in one step, here 0.2 Å.
`StopNorm::MaxAtom` makes `grad_norm` the largest per-atom force, the same measure as `fmax` in the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE), so the stop test is 0.01 eV/Å on every atom.
FIRE runs through the same loop.
Only the `Method` and `istep` change; for FIRE, `istep` is the initial time step.

## Read the result

#+CAPTION: Largest per-atom force against force calls on the Pt256 Morse start.
[[file:../../figures/relax-morse/convergence.png]]

All three methods reach the same minimum: the final energies agree to within 0.000705 eV.
L-BFGS gets there in 11 force calls: its first step used three and every later step one.
FIRE used one call per step plus one for the start, 51 in all.
FIRE 2.0 took fewer steps, 42, and 46 calls.

To redraw the figure from a fresh run:

```bash
python3 docs/figures/relax-morse/plot_convergence.py
```

## Try next

- Change `FMAX` in `examples/relax_morse.rs` and see how the gap between L-BFGS and FIRE moves.
- Point `read_con` at `tests/data/morse_pos_0008.con`, the second fixture.
- Read @@rst::doc:`hold a stateful solver <../howto/session>`@@ for the setters a host can call, and @@rst::doc:`the secant family <../explanation/quasi-newton>`@@ for why a capped L-BFGS step behaves as it does.

If you use `rgmin` in published work, cite it with the repository's `CITATION.cff`.
@@rst::doc:`../howto/cite`@@ shows how to add the version you ran.

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/rlbfgs.org`

# Cautious Riemannian L-BFGS

`minimize_rlbfgs` is Algorithm 2 of Huang, Absil, and Gallivan, /A Riemannian BFGS Method Without Differentiated Retraction for Nonconvex Optimization Problems/, SIAM J. Optim. 28 (2018) 470–495 ([10.1137/17M1127582](https://doi.org/10.1137/17M1127582)). The two-loop inverse Hessian is Huang, Gallivan, and Absil 2015 ([10.1137/140955483](https://doi.org/10.1137/140955483)). On a Euclidean manifold the transport is the identity, so the update is the cautious BFGS method of Li and Fukushima 2001 ([10.1137/S1052623499354242](https://doi.org/10.1137/S1052623499354242)).

`Rlbfgs::default` is the section 7 choice: four pairs, `vartheta(t) = 10^{-4} t`, Armijo constant `10^{-4}`, backtrack one half, and the stop `||grad|| / ||grad_0|| < 10^{-6}`. A pair that fails the cautious test is not stored. The line search does not differentiate the retraction. The vector transport is the parallel transport along the exponential when the manifold provides that pair, and the retraction transport otherwise.

This does not replace `Lbfgs`. The production Euclidean step stays `LbfgsStep::Capped` at `EON_MAX_MOVE`.

```rust
use ndarray::{ArrayView1, array};
use rgmin::{Control, ManifoldKind, Oracle, Rlbfgs, minimize_rlbfgs};

let obj = Oracle::unbounded(2, |x: ArrayView1<f64>| {
    let value = 0.5 * (x[0] * x[0] + 100.0 * x[1] * x[1]);
    let grad = array![x[0], 100.0 * x[1]];
    (value, grad)
});
let report = minimize_rlbfgs(
    &ManifoldKind::Euclidean,
    &obj,
    array![1.0, 1.0],
    &Control::default().with_maxiter(12).with_gtol(0.0),
    &Rlbfgs::default(),
)?;
assert!(report.converged());
```

The quadratic is the Euclidean reduction. Its minimizer has value 0. Section 7.2 is the relative gradient stop used above. On the sphere the same solver is the joint diagonalization cost of section 7.1, `-(x^T C x)^2`, whose diagonalizer for `C = diag(3, 2, 1)` has cost `-9`.

The C record is `rgmin_rlbfgs_t`. Null parameters select the Rust default. `rgmin_minimize_rlbfgs` takes the session manifold token. ABI minor 51.

---

Source: `docs/orgmode/tutorials/scg.org`

# Scaled conjugate gradient

Møller SCG prices the step with a damped model. There is no line search. A positive finite `Control::maxmove` bounds every trial, including the retry after a non-finite value. Zero, negative, infinite and NaN leave the step unbounded.

The listing is `examples/tutorial_scg.rs`, whole. Continuous integration runs it, so it is the program as it builds.

Source: `../../../examples/tutorial_scg.rs`

The example calls `minimize_scg` on a quadratic and checks both coordinates.
